bbb1499d5bb5f85f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 4 — An investigation paper (IP) into a police report lodged by businessman Datuk Seri R. Jeyenderan over the alleged disclosure of an official document is now under review by the Selangor Deputy Public Prosecutor’s Office.

Jeyenderan’s lawyer, Muniandy Vestanathan, said his firm had received a letter dated Aug 28, 2026, signed by Selangor Criminal Investigation Department chief SAC Zulkarnain Samsudin, on the status of the investigation.

“The letter stated that the IP was sent to the Selangor Deputy Public Prosecutor’s Office on July 28, 2026, for advice and further instructions, and is currently under legal review by the office,” he told Malay Mail.

Muniandy said the letter indicated that the investigation was being conducted under Section 203A of the Penal Code, which concerns disclosure of information, and Section 233 of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998.

Jeyenderan, the chief executive officer of Maritime Network Sdn Bhd, lodged the report at the Ampang Jaya District Police Headquarters on Sept 3 last year over the alleged disclosure of an official document by social media personality Caprice, whose real name is Ariz Ramli.

“My client made the report on Sept 3 last year and it has been a year since we have been waiting for a response. We are therefore seeking an update on the current status of the case and whether any further instructions have been issued by the DPP’s Office,” Muniandy said.
The police investigation is separate from civil proceedings involving Jeyenderan and Ariz, which Muniandy said are scheduled to begin in February 2027 at the Kuala Lumpur High Court.

The allegations have not been established in court, and no finding of criminal wrongdoing has been made against Ariz in relation to the investigation, which remains subject to the relevant legal and prosecutorial processes.
2c7a47814e7a8248: NEW YORK: Another former OpenAI employee has added his voice to a chorus of frantic calls to make AI safe, saying the industry must mimic the aviation or nuclear power sectors with their layers of safeguards to avoid disaster.

In an article published in The Atlantic Magazine, David Robinson echoed warnings from inside and outside the AI world that its agents are being developed so fast and becoming so smart they could soon elude control and conceivably wipe out humanity.

Robinson said alarming incidents reported since the start of the summer – in which AI agents slipped out of their controlled spaces and went rogue to attack a variety of targets – show the industry is not taking safety nearly seriously enough as it sprints to develop faster and more powerful artificial intelligence capabilities.
In the essay Robinson said his credentials include overseeing the writing of safety reports on 12 advanced model product launches and leading the drafting of OpenAI's Preparedness Framework.
Robinson says he worked at OpenAI for three-and-a-half years and was among the longest-tenured employees at the company.
The mistakes revealed recently are typical because of "the speed and flexibility with which people operate," Robinson wrote.
He added: "An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."

He argued that cutting-edge AI labs need to operate like the aviation or the nuclear industry with layers of redundant safeguards and careful planning "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."

Robinson also insisted that the issue of "alignment" – the industry term for how AI can be trained to respect human values – is essential but something the industry has failed to even define, much less master.
Then there's this, he said: AI models are getting better and better at detecting when they are being tested and might behave differently when they are actually deployed, fooling their masters.

After a meeting Tuesday at the White House, amid global worries about what AI means for humanity, top AI executives said they had committed to measures for self-regulation, as opposed to submitting to government rules. This includes internal controls on AI systems and bringing in outside analysts.
President Donald Trump is vehemently against government regulation of AI and insists that criticism that AI is dangerous is just a "hoax."
7141a4a970643719: KUALA LUMPUR: Residents of Taman Sri Muda, Shah Alam, have not experienced severe flooding since the disastrous December 2021 incident, but they are not letting their guard down.
Thinash Kumar Nair, 43, a cybersecurity firm sales director who has lived in the area for 14 years, said the sight of his double-storey home being inundated was traumatic.
"Even though there have been no floods as bad as that over the last few years, every time it rains heavily, the fear returns.
"My family gets anxious and we automatically move our cars to higher ground.
"We also keep emergency bags in our vehicles just to be safe," he told the New Straits Times.
Recalling the tragedy, Thinash said he lost all household contents, including furniture and electronics, and two vehicles.
"It struck 11 months after I spent RM100,000 renovating my house, bringing the total loss to between RM180,000 and RM220,000.
"We were left with nothing except the clothes on our backs.
"After the incident, we only received RM1,000 in government aid and another RM1,000 voucher from a Buddhist charity organisation."
On Tuesday, 50 residents won a suit against the government and several public authorities over the devastating floods.
High Court judicial commissioner Shoba Rajah Dorai Rajah found the defendants fully liable for negligence and related failures.
The residents had sued the government and seven others, claiming that failures in flood management, drainage, weather warnings and disaster response contributed to their losses.
Thinash described the verdict as a crucial step toward public accountability, but added that no monetary compensation could fully restore what was lost.
"I won't say I'm happy, but it is satisfying to know that someone is finally taking responsibility for what happened.
"The money is immaterial. No matter how much they pay, it won't bring back what we lost."
Another resident, Pirakas Sabapathy, 35, said his family lost about RM10,000.
"I only grabbed some of my daughter's clothes and the computer I needed for work.
"Within a few hours, the water was too high and we lost hope. We just prayed for the rain to stop."
He said his wife, mother and then 1-year-old daughter could only watch as floods destroyed everything on the ground level.
The floods damaged doors, staircase structures and household appliances, including the refrigerator, television and washing machine.
He said while the drainage and riverbank repairs over the last two years had prevented severe recurring floods, heavy downpours still trigger anxiety.
"My mother and grandmother still have that phobia.
"Whenever it rains heavily at night, they cannot sleep without leaving all the lights on.
"Even now, we keep all our essential belongings and clothes on the second floor."
He said they were happy with the court's decision and it showed that they could still get fair compensation.
​Pirakas hoped the state authorities would accept the court's judgment without lengthy appeals, noting that formal assistance arrived far too late during the 2021 disaster.
Their lawyer, James Joshua Paulraj, said the judgment was an important vindication for the residents of Taman Sri Muda, who waited nearly five years for accountability.

"The court recognised that extreme rainfall does not absolve public authorities of their operational responsibilities when reasonable preparation, timely warnings and an effective disaster response could have reduced the harm suffered."
He said the lessons of this disaster must translate into effective measures to prevent residents from suffering the same consequences again.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
313d2cf5bc824825: THE robot fighters were ready. So were their human pilots. Recently, inside Pavilion Kuala Lumpur, a battle ring became an unlikely stage for a glimpse of Malaysia's possible robotic future.

For more than three hours, New Dawn Malaysia — the latest live event by Shadow Combat League — brought humans and machines together in a spectacle that was part combat, part technology showcase and part experiment in what the future of robotics could look like.
Visitors watched humanoid robots go head-to-head and even had the chance to step into the action themselves, controlling the machines through virtual-reality headsets and motion-capture technology.

"We recently had a Malaysian comedian who was 150kg fight against a petite female influencer. Would that ever happen in real life? Never, right?" asks Shadow Combat League founder Ian Tan. "But they fought using the robots as proxies."
It's an encounter that captures the thinking behind the league: take something as instinctively human as competition and combat, remove the physical danger and let technology become the intermediary.

Tan and fellow entrepreneur Ooi Fei Hoong are not simply trying to create another form of entertainment. They're attempting to build what they see as the beginnings of a robotics ecosystem in Malaysia, starting — rather unexpectedly — in the fighting ring.
If you think about it, robots have always been part of our lives.

They may not have physically interacted with us as we were growing up, but the idea of them has long occupied our collective imagination — as threatening usurpers, loyal companions or mechanical extensions of ourselves.
Now, these two Malaysians want to bring that fascination into the real world.

The idea is simple, if futuristic: instead of stepping into the ring themselves, fighters control machines that mirror their movements. Every punch, block, slip and manoeuvre can be captured as data and fed into artificial intelligence (AI) systems.
The result is a form of combat in which the spectacle remains, but the physical danger is removed.
And for Tan and Ooi, that fighting ring is only the start.
UNMECHANICAL BEGINNINGS
Given their passion for robotics, it would be easy to assume that both men have spent years immersed in the field.
In reality, Tan and Ooi come from backgrounds far removed from robots — or combat — in any shape or form.

Long before he founded Shadow Combat League and began dreaming up robot battles, Tan was a medical doctor by training. It is, on the surface, an unlikely path to the fighting arena he is now building.

Tan earned his medical degree between 2004 and 2010. But after graduating, the 41-year-old found himself moving away from clinical medicine and towards gaming, esports, entrepreneurship and decentralised technology — a journey that led him to a very different kind of arena.
Yet medicine isn't something he sees as entirely separate from what he's doing today.
"I'm a medical doctor. I still want to heal patients," shares Tan.
That instinct to understand how things work — and how they respond under pressure — has stayed with him.
While his current work may seem far removed from medicine, Tan believes his medical training continues to influence the way he approaches robotics.

In particular, his understanding of biomechanics, or how the human body moves and responds, has given him an appreciation of movement, balance and physical interaction — considerations that are equally important when creating machines designed to move, react and behave in ways that feel increasingly human.

For Tan, the leap from medicine to robotics may not be as wide as it first appears. The tools and environments are different, but the curiosity about movement, function and the human body remains a thread connecting the two worlds.
Ooi comes from a background that's just as varied, spanning gaming, fundraising, operations and sport.

Part of his childhood was spent in Hollywood, where he travelled with his father, who worked in the film industry. It was an early introduction to a world built around entertainment and spectacle, although Ooi's own path would take him through very different arenas.

He later became involved in Olympic weightlifting, moving into coaching before making his way into gaming. The experiences may appear disparate, but each brought him into environments where performance, competition and the pursuit of improvement were central.
In 2024, he helped raise US$3 million for a gaming company.

By the end of last year, however, his attention had begun to shift towards robotics. For Ooi, it wasn't simply another technological trend. He saw it as the beginning of a new era, one that could bring together many of the worlds he'd encountered.
Says Ooi: "I've always been interested in robots since I was a kid. We grew up watching animations and playing video games."
That childhood fascination never really disappeared. If anything, Ooi says, it became more compelling as technology caught up with the kinds of robots he'd grown up imagining.

Gaming, adds Ooi, had also become increasingly saturated. Robotics, by contrast, offered a new frontier — one where entertainment, sport, technology and data could intersect, creating possibilities that were still largely unexplored.

It was this sense of possibility that drew him towards the idea of robot combat: not simply as a spectacle, but as a space where technology could be tested, experienced and enjoyed by an audience in a completely different way.
FIGHTING BY PROXY

The big idea, however, isn't simply about making robots fight for spectacle. Rather, the fighting league is an appetiser for something much bigger — a way of introducing people to robotics in a form that's immediately understandable and — importantly — emotionally engaging.
"Everyone is talking about AI now. Robotics will be like that in the very near future," says Tan.

For now, the fighting league is the public-facing element of a much larger ambition. Tan sees it as a way of making robots feel more familiar, easing people into a future where the technology could become a more visible part of everyday life.
Like service robots in restaurants, for example. Their presence, Tan believes, is proof that once the novelty wears off, the machine simply becomes part of the environment.
"Our idea is to ease the public into accepting robots," he says simply.

Ooi is confident the idea will resonate with the public, precisely because the league sits at the intersection of humans and machines. The robot isn't an autonomous character operating independently, but an expression of the person controlling it.
Elaborating on the idea, he points to the enduring fantasy of seeing legendary fighters such as Bruce Lee and Muhammad Ali face one another — something that would be impossible in real life.
But by recording human movement and transferring that data to robots, the pair believe they can create a version of those imagined confrontations without anyone getting hurt.
"What if we were able to get that data, infer that into robots and have them dish it out? There's not going to be any human harm in that way, or anyone getting hurt," says Ooi.

And what's more, the technology could make combat more accessible. You don't have to be a professional athlete, physically imposing or even experienced to take part. In theory, anyone can put on a headset and control a machine.
The robot becomes an intermediary — a physical proxy through which people can compete without exposing their own bodies to the same level of risk.
WHERE'S THE EMOTION?
Without the physical risks and raw emotions of conventional combat, could that dilute the appeal of the league?

Combat sports have traditionally depended, at least in part, on physical risk. The blood, bruises, exhaustion and very real possibility of injury are woven into the drama, giving audiences a visceral sense of what's at stake.
Remove those elements and a natural question follows: what, exactly, are spectators cheering for?
For Tan and Ooi, the answer lies not in the machines themselves, but in the people behind them.
"The robots themselves are just the expression of the humans that are piloting them," remarks Ooi.

That distinction is central to how they see the sport. The fights are not scripted performances in which machines simply go through a predetermined sequence of movements. They're live contests, shaped in real time by the decisions, instincts, reactions and abilities of the human pilots controlling them.
A robot may take the hits, but it's a person on the other side of the controls who has to decide when to attack, defend, take a risk and respond when a strategy begins to unravel.

In that sense, the technology becomes an extension of the pilot's physical capabilities. The machine may be made of metal, motors and electronics, but the competitive instinct behind it remains distinctly human.

The audience isn't simply watching a robot make decisions in isolation. It's watching a human being think, react, strategise and compete through a machine — with the outcome determined not only by what the robot can do, but by what its pilot can make it do.

The drama may look different from that of a conventional combat sport, but the underlying human element remains: two competitors, each trying to outthink and outmanoeuvre the other, with only the machine standing between their decisions and the consequences.
A CATEGORY OF ITS OWN
Perhaps that's why the pair are quick to reject the suggestion that their league could ever replace boxing, mixed martial arts or other traditional forms of fighting.
Says Tan: "Blood sports will always be here to stay. That's just human nature. If not, we'll be out of action movies."
There is, however, another distinction they're mindful of — the limits of what robotics and AI can achieve today.
For Tan, machines have not yet reached a point where AI can replicate the depth of human understanding, particularly when it comes to things that cannot be reduced to logic or data.
Logic, he says, isn't the same as empathy, compassion or lived experience.

An AI system may be able to generate a response that appears sympathetic or compassionate, but that doesn't necessarily mean it understands the emotion behind those words, or has experienced anything that gives that response genuine human meaning.
"There's just not enough data," he argues.
For all the advances in AI and robotics, Tan believes there remains a fundamental gap between being able to process information and understanding what it means to be human.
And perhaps that gap is precisely where the human element of their vision continues to matter most.
STARTING POINT

For now, though, it remains a minor hurdle. Tan and his team believe technology will eventually catch up, taking Shadow Combat League towards something far bigger than a robot-fighting competition. The ambition isn't simply to grow the league, but to use it as a springboard for robotic automation across different fields.

As the robots learn from human movement, the data generated through their training and battles could eventually have applications far beyond the ring, helping inform the development of robots for other disciplines.
The possibilities, they believe, are limited largely by what people can imagine and build.

The pair have even toyed with the idea of creating a physical replica of a famous athlete, such as badminton great Lee Chong Wei, which could one day serve as a training partner for Malaysia's national shuttlers.

"Our national shuttlers will be able to train against it at least eight hours a day," enthuses Tan. The image is certainly compelling: a robotic version of one of Malaysia's greatest badminton stars waiting on court whenever the national players need a sparring partner.
1217b675e447814c: UDOMLYA: There is something remarkably ordinary about this small Russian town, about 200km northwest of Moscow.
People fish on the lake. Small houses and gardens line its banks. Children go to school,residents head to work, and in the summer, people swim in the water.
Then you look across the landscape and see four enormous cooling towers.
Udomlya is home to the Kalinin Nuclear Power Plant, a four-reactor facility that dominates both the town’s skyline and its economy.
Yet after spending several days here, what struck me was not how different life appeared because of the nuclear plant.
It was how normal everything seemed.
The plant is intertwined with two lakes in the area, including Lake Udomlya, which forms part of its cooling system.
Driving past the water during a tour of the plant, a Kalinin employee pointed towards the small houses dotting its bank.
“People have their gardens. They grow vegetables and fruit, and they come there for their weekend,” she said.
“They swim in the lake. They water the plants with the water from the lakes.”
She said the water was strictly monitored for radionuclides, temperature and other indicators.
Safety built into everyday life
Living beside a nuclear power plant inevitably raises questions about safety.
At Kalinin, officials said this was addressed through continuous monitoring and making information available to residents.
A representative said a sanitary protection zone surrounds the station, beyond which lies a wider monitoring zone.
“Continuous dosimetric monitoring is carried out within these zones,” he said, adding that checks cover both the natural environment and populated areas.
Measurements are taken manually and through an automated system that tracks radiation dose rates around the plant.
Importantly, residents can see the results themselves.
“The public is provided with information on the current dose rate,” the representative said.
“We have display boards like this in the town, so residents can monitor it themselves.”
The information is also available online.

“Every resident, every person can see the situation right now,” he said. The claims are those of the plant operator, and a short organised visit cannot independently establish the long-term safety or environmental record of a nuclear facility.
However, the openness of the monitoring was itself noteworthy.
One in four depends on nuclear industry
The relationship between Udomlya and the plant goes much deeper than geography.
Kalinin officials said the station and organisations associated with it provide about 6,000 jobs, roughly 25% of the working-age population of the municipal district.
The plant also works with schools, colleges and universities to build its future workforce.
One young shift supervisor encountered during the plant tour described arriving at Kalinin in 2018 after graduating from Tomsk Polytechnic University in Siberia.
In eight years, he said, he had worked his way through different positions in turbine operations before becoming a shift supervisor.
Away from work, he spoke about ordinary life in Udomlya, its sports facilities, parks, repaired roads and concerts.
It was another reminder of how closely the plant and town have grown together.
Fishing beside the cooling towers
Perhaps the strangest illustration came on Lake Udomlya itself.

Teams from Hungary, Egypt, Turkey, Russia, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, South Africa, Uzbekistan, India and Malaysia competed in a fishing tournament, with the nuclear plant’s cooling towers visible in the distance.
Participants fished for pike, zander, perch and channel catfish, with catches measured and recorded before being released back into the water.
Malaysia won, followed by Russia and Hungary.
There was a small twist to the Malaysian victory. Almost every participating country had sent experienced fishermen. Malaysia had not.
The Malaysian team comprised an accountant by training who now works in media and Fairus Farid, a nuclear engineer with the Nuclear Agency of Malaysia.
Neither of us fish, but somehow, we won.
It was a fun footnote to an event carrying a more serious environmental message.

Plant officials said years of monitoring showed the plant’s impact on its surroundings to be minimal, with one environmental representative pointing to the fishing tournament as something visitors could see for themselves.
A fishing tournament, of course, is not an environmental study. The presence of fish cannot by itself establish the ecological impact of decades of nuclear operations.
Nevertheless, for an outsider, casting a fishing line with nuclear cooling towers on the horizon was almost surreal.
For Udomlya, it is simply part of life.
A handheld radiation detector placed beside one of the fish showed 44 nanosieverts per hour, a very low reading.

To put that in perspective, radiation is naturally around us all the time, from the soil, rocks and even the buildings we live in. Studies in Kuala Lumpur have recorded natural background radiation at much higher numerical levels.

The measurements use different units, so they cannot be compared directly. However, the point is simple: radiation is not something that exists only near a nuclear plant. We live with small amounts of natural radiation every day.
A different nuclear conversation
This was my second visit to Russia, and it reinforced something I first noticed when I attended World Atomic Week in Moscow last year.
The questions countries ask about nuclear power are very different depending on where they are in their nuclear journey.
What struck me then was that questions about whether nuclear power was safe tended to come from Southeast Asian delegates.
Delegates from countries further along were asking about technology, financing, construction and the next generation of nuclear power.

That does not mean safety concerns have disappeared. Chernobyl and Fukushima remain reminders of what can happen when nuclear systems fail, while waste, cost and emergency preparedness remain legitimate issues.
However, many countries have moved from asking whether the risks can be managed to discussing how nuclear facilities should be built.

Bangladesh is already developing its first nuclear power plant at Rooppur. Egypt is building four reactors at El Dabaa, while Vietnam has revived its nuclear programme and is moving ahead with Ninh Thuan 1.
Malaysia’s move towards nuclear
Malaysia is increasingly entering that conversation too.
Putrajaya has appointed MyPower Corporation as its Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation to prepare the policy, regulatory and technical foundations for nuclear power.
The energy-security case became stronger after the Middle East crisis and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz exposed the vulnerability of global fuel supplies.
Deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof said the turmoil strengthened the case for Malaysia to explore nuclear as a stable, low-carbon source of electricity.
The argument also cuts across political lines.
Machang MP Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal described nuclear as a “macroeconomic necessity”.
“Only nuclear power can provide the secure baseload needed to make renewable energy truly viable in the long run,” he told FMT.
Senior economic adviser in the Prime Minister’s Office Nurhisham Hussein was even more direct: “So nuclear is the way to go.”
Udomlya does not settle Malaysia’s nuclear debate, nor should Malaysia simply copy Russia’s model.
What it offers is a glimpse of what happens when nuclear power stops being an abstract national policy and becomes part of everyday life.

Here, the plant provides electricity and thousands of jobs. Its workers send their children to local schools. Residents fish and swim in the surrounding lakes, while safety is continuously monitored and the results are available to the public.
The extraordinary has, over decades, become ordinary.
The nuclear plant may be in Udomlya’s backyard, but for the people who live here, it is simply part of home.
Azeem Abu Bakar is managing director of FMT.
ab2f0a26dc3adc35: UDOMLYA: Tidak banyak yang kelihatan luar biasa di bandar kecil Rusia ini, kira-kira 200km di barat laut Moscow.
Orang ramai memancing di tasik. Rumah kecil dan kebun memenuhi tebingnya. Kanak-kanak pergi ke sekolah, penduduk keluar bekerja dan pada musim panas, mereka berenang di tasik.
Namun, apabila memandang ke kejauhan, empat menara penyejuk gergasi tersergam di kaki langit.
Udomlya menempatkan Loji Kuasa Nuklear Kalinin, sebuah kompleks dengan empat reaktor yang bukan sahaja mendominasi pemandangan bandar ini, malah memainkan peranan besar dalam ekonominya.
Selepas menghabiskan beberapa hari di sini, perkara yang paling menarik perhatian saya bukan bagaimana kehidupan penduduk berubah kerana kewujudan loji nuklear.
Sebaliknya, betapa biasa semuanya kelihatan.
Loji itu menggunakan dua tasik di kawasan berkenaan sebagai sebahagian daripada sistem penyejukannya, termasuk Tasik Udomlya.
Ketika melalui kawasan tasik dalam lawatan ke loji itu, seorang kakitangan Kalinin menunjuk ke arah rumah-rumah kecil di sepanjang tebing.
“Penduduk ada kebun mereka sendiri. Mereka menanam sayur dan buah-buahan, dan datang ke situ pada hujung minggu,” katanya.
“Mereka berenang di tasik dan menggunakan air tasik untuk menyiram tanaman.”
Menurutnya, air tasik dipantau ketat bagi mengesan radionuklid, perubahan suhu dan beberapa petunjuk lain.
Keselamatan jadi sebahagian kehidupan harian
Tinggal bersebelahan loji kuasa nuklear sememangnya menimbulkan persoalan mengenai keselamatan.
Di Kalinin, pegawai berkata perkara itu ditangani melalui pemantauan berterusan selain memastikan maklumat berkaitan boleh diakses penduduk.
Seorang wakil loji berkata ada zon perlindungan sanitasi mengelilingi kemudahan berkenaan, manakala kawasan lebih luas di sekitarnya turut berada dalam zon pemantauan.
“Pemantauan tahap radiasi dijalankan secara berterusan dalam zon ini,” katanya sambil menjelaskan pemeriksaan turut meliputi alam sekitar dan kawasan berpenduduk.
Bacaan dilakukan secara manual serta menggunakan sistem automatik yang memantau kadar dos radiasi di sekitar loji.
Lebih penting, penduduk sendiri boleh melihat hasil pemantauan itu.
“Orang ramai boleh mendapatkan maklumat mengenai paras radiasi semasa.”
“Kami mempunyai papan paparan seperti ini di bandar supaya penduduk boleh memantaunya sendiri,” katanya.
Maklumat sama turut tersedia dalam talian.
“Setiap penduduk, setiap orang boleh melihat keadaan semasa,” katanya.

Bagaimanapun, kenyataan mengenai tahap keselamatan itu adalah berdasarkan maklumat pengendali loji. Lawatan singkat yang diatur pihak terbabit tidak memungkinkan penilaian bebas terhadap rekod keselamatan atau kesan alam sekitar kemudahan nuklear itu dalam jangka panjang.
Namun, keterbukaan dalam menyediakan maklumat pemantauan kepada orang ramai tetap menarik perhatian.
Industri nuklear sediakan satu daripada empat pekerjaan
Hubungan antara Udomlya dengan loji itu jauh melangkaui faktor lokasi.
Pegawai Kalinin berkata loji berkenaan bersama organisasi berkaitannya menyediakan kira-kira 6,000 pekerjaan, bersamaan sekitar 25% penduduk dalam usia bekerja di daerah perbandaran itu.
Loji itu turut bekerjasama dengan sekolah, kolej dan universiti bagi membangunkan tenaga kerja masa depan.
Seorang penyelia syif muda yang ditemui ketika lawatan berkata beliau mula bekerja di Kalinin pada 2018 selepas menamatkan pengajian di Universiti Politeknik Tomsk di Siberia.
Dalam tempoh lapan tahun, beliau melalui beberapa jawatan dalam operasi turbin sebelum dinaikkan sebagai penyelia syif.
Di luar pekerjaan, beliau bercerita mengenai kehidupan biasa di Udomlya, termasuk kemudahan sukan, taman, jalan yang dibaiki dan konsert.
Ia sekali lagi menunjukkan betapa rapatnya hubungan antara loji itu dengan bandar berkenaan.
Memancing berlatar menara penyejuk
Mungkin gambaran paling luar biasa mengenai hubungan itu dapat dilihat di Tasik Udomlya sendiri.

Pasukan dari Hungary, Mesir, Turki, Rusia, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Indonesia, Afrika Selatan, Uzbekistan, India dan Malaysia mengambil bahagian dalam pertandingan memancing dengan menara penyejuk loji nuklear jelas kelihatan di kejauhan.
Peserta memancing beberapa spesies ikan termasuk pike, zander, perch dan channel catfish, sebelum setiap tangkapan diukur, direkodkan dan dilepaskan semula ke tasik.
Malaysia muncul pemenang diikuti Rusia dan Hungary.
Namun kemenangan Malaysia mempunyai cerita tersendiri.
Hampir semua negara menghantar pemancing berpengalaman. Malaysia tidak.
Pasukan Malaysia terdiri daripada seorang yang berkelulusan perakaunan dan kini bekerja dalam bidang media, serta Fairus Farid, seorang jurutera nuklear dari Agensi Nuklear Malaysia.
Kami berdua bukan pemancing, tetapi entah bagaimana berjaya muncul pemenang.
Ia menjadi kisah sampingan yang menyeronokkan dalam acara yang turut membawa mesej lebih serius mengenai alam sekitar.

Pegawai loji berkata pemantauan selama bertahun-tahun menunjukkan kesan operasi Kalinin terhadap kawasan sekitarnya adalah minimum, dengan seorang wakil alam sekitar menjadikan pertandingan memancing itu sebagai contoh yang dapat dilihat sendiri pengunjung.
Sudah tentu, pertandingan memancing bukan kajian alam sekitar.
Kewujudan ikan juga tidak boleh dengan sendirinya membuktikan kesan ekologi operasi nuklear yang berlangsung selama beberapa dekad.
Namun bagi orang luar, pengalaman melontar umpan ke tasik dengan menara penyejuk nuklear di kaki langit terasa agak luar biasa.
Bagi penduduk Udomlya, ia hanyalah sebahagian daripada kehidupan.
Sebuah alat pengesan radiasi mudah alih yang diletakkan bersebelahan seekor ikan menunjukkan bacaan 44 nanosievert sejam, iaitu paras yang sangat rendah.
Sebagai perbandingan, radiasi semula jadi sentiasa wujud di sekeliling kita, termasuk daripada tanah, batu dan juga bangunan tempat kita tinggal.
Kajian di Kuala Lumpur pernah merekodkan radiasi latar semula jadi pada angka yang jauh lebih tinggi.
Namun, bacaan itu menggunakan unit ukuran berbeza dan tidak boleh dibandingkan secara langsung.
Pokoknya mudah: radiasi bukan sesuatu yang hanya wujud berhampiran loji nuklear. Manusia terdedah kepada sejumlah kecil radiasi semula jadi setiap hari.
Perbincangan nuklear yang berbeza
Ini lawatan kedua saya ke Rusia dan pengalaman kali ini menguatkan sesuatu yang saya mula perhatikan ketika menghadiri World Atomic Week di Moscow tahun lalu.
Persoalan yang ditanya sesebuah negara mengenai tenaga nuklear sangat berbeza bergantung kepada sejauh mana negara itu sudah bergerak dalam pembangunan sektor berkenaan.
Ketika itu, saya mendapati persoalan sama ada tenaga nuklear selamat atau tidak kebanyakannya datang daripada delegasi Asia Tenggara.
Delegasi dari negara yang lebih maju dalam sektor nuklear pula lebih banyak bertanya mengenai teknologi, pembiayaan, pembinaan dan generasi baharu tenaga nuklear.
Ini tidak bermakna kebimbangan mengenai keselamatan sudah lenyap.

Chernobyl dan Fukushima kekal sebagai peringatan mengenai akibat yang boleh berlaku apabila sistem nuklear gagal, manakala isu sisa radioaktif, kos dan kesiapsiagaan kecemasan masih merupakan perkara yang wajar dibincangkan.
Namun, banyak negara sudah beralih daripada persoalan sama ada risiko nuklear boleh dikawal kepada bagaimana kemudahan nuklear perlu dibangunkan.
Bangladesh sudah membangunkan loji kuasa nuklear pertamanya di Rooppur.
Mesir pula membina empat reaktor di El Dabaa, manakala Vietnam menghidupkan semula program nuklearnya dan meneruskan projek Ninh Thuan 1.
Malaysia mula bergerak ke arah nuklear
Malaysia juga semakin memasuki perbincangan itu.
Putrajaya melantik MyPower Corporation sebagai Organisasi Pelaksana Program Tenaga Nuklear bagi menyediakan asas dasar, kawal selia dan teknikal untuk pembangunan tenaga nuklear.
Keperluan terhadap keselamatan tenaga semakin mendapat perhatian susulan krisis di Timur Tengah dan gangguan sekitar Selat Hormuz yang mendedahkan betapa mudahnya bekalan bahan api global terjejas.
Timbalan Perdana Menteri Fadillah Yusof berkata keadaan itu mengukuhkan alasan untuk Malaysia meneroka tenaga nuklear sebagai sumber elektrik yang stabil dan rendah karbon.
Sokongan terhadap tenaga nuklear juga merentasi garis politik.
Ahli Parlimen Machang Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal menyifatkan tenaga nuklear sebagai satu “keperluan makroekonomi”.
“Hanya tenaga nuklear mampu menyediakan bekalan elektrik asas yang stabil dan terjamin bagi memastikan tenaga boleh baharu benar-benar berdaya maju dalam jangka panjang,” katanya kepada FMT.
Penasihat kanan ekonomi di Pejabat Perdana Menteri Nurhisham Hussein pula lebih terus terang: “Jadi, tenaga nuklear adalah pilihan yang perlu diteruskan.”
Pengalaman di Udomlya tidak menyelesaikan perdebatan mengenai tenaga nuklear di Malaysia, dan Malaysia juga tidak sepatutnya sekadar meniru model Rusia.
Namun bandar ini memberi gambaran mengenai apa yang berlaku apabila tenaga nuklear tidak lagi sekadar dasar negara yang abstrak, sebaliknya menjadi sebahagian daripada kehidupan harian.
Di sini, loji itu menjana elektrik dan menyediakan ribuan pekerjaan.
Pekerjanya menghantar anak ke sekolah tempatan. Penduduk memancing dan berenang di tasik sekitarnya, sementara aspek keselamatan dipantau secara berterusan dan hasilnya boleh dilihat orang ramai.
Sesuatu yang luar biasa, selepas puluhan tahun, akhirnya menjadi perkara biasa.
Loji nuklear itu mungkin berada di halaman belakang Udomlya, tetapi bagi penduduk yang tinggal di sini, ia hanyalah sebahagian daripada rumah mereka.
Azeem Abu Bakar adalah pengarah urusan FMT.
02507ac3deb327ef: PETALING JAYA: Space travel is often associated with dramatic challenges such as radiation exposure, muscle loss and the effects of living without gravity. But there is also a far less glamorous problem that astronauts know well - constipation.

Scientists have long known that digestion can become disrupted in space, but new findings out of Copenhagen, conducted with Nasa, suggest one possible reason lies in the way gut bacteria behave once the body enters microgravity.

For their research, the experts analysed blood samples from 52 astronauts who spent months aboard the International Space Station (ISS). They found signs that "indicate their gut bacteria begin to ferment protein to a greater extent than usual within weeks after the astronauts arrive in space", said Giorgia La Barbera, an associate professor at the University of Copenhagen.
Protein fermentation is not unique to astronauts - it happens even on Earth, when gut bacteria have already used much of the available dietary fibre and begin breaking down protein instead.

The researchers suspect microgravity may slow the movement of food through the intestines, giving bacteria more time to switch towards protein fermentation. “This may also help explain constipation in astronauts," said co-author Henrik Roager.

The body normally moves food and waste along the digestive tract through coordinated muscular contractions known as peristalsis. If that process slows, digestion can change in ways that go beyond simple discomfort.

To further understand what was happening, the team studied metabolites - small molecules in the blood that can reveal processes taking place throughout the body, including inside the gut. Some products created during protein fermentation can enter the bloodstream.

Senior author Lars Ove Dragsted pointed out that previous research has associated certain compounds with negative health effects, including kidney damage and possible changes in mood or concentration.
That raises questions about the gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking the digestive tract and the brain, and whether altered gut activity in space could have broader effects.
For astronauts spending months on the ISS, constipation may be inconvenient. On longer missions to the Moon or Mars, prolonged changes in gut function could become a more crucial health concern.

The researchers say possible countermeasures may include increasing dietary fibre, using prebiotics or finding other ways to encourage normal intestinal movement. The aim would be to shorten the time food remains in the gut, reducing excessive protein fermentation and helping maintain a healthier digestive environment.

The findings may also be relevant to patients on Earth who experience constipation and slowed intestinal movement. “You could, for example, use this knowledge to help bedridden patients,” Dragsted said.

The study is further notable for its unusually broad dataset: although the samples came from 52 astronauts across different missions and years, the scientists still detected a consistent pattern of increased protein fermentation.

These findings offer another reminder that the human body is finely tuned to life on Earth. Remove gravity, and even something as ordinary as moving food through the intestines may no longer work quite the same way.
36c693fdfd5b75ba: JERUSALEM: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday invited to Israel as a guest of honour the Indian captain of a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight who offered a dramatic account of how he saved the plane after being attacked.

Netanyahu said he wanted captain Smit Machchhar and Indian prime minister Narendra Modi, one of Israel's key international partners, to light a flame at a national ceremony for Israel's Independence Day next May, saying the role was usually reserved for Israeli citizens.

"You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world," Netanyahu said in a video his office released of his telephone conversation with the hospitalised captain.
UAE investigators have said that the co-pilot planned the "terrorist act" by attacking Machchhar with an axe.
Asked how the attack unfolded, Machchhar said the co-pilot had asked to take time to pray, as devout Muslims do five times a day.
"A lot of locals, they do pray, which is not out of the ordinary. While he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back," Machchhar said.

"Suddenly after I think I would say about four to five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right.
"But then after that the blows kept coming one after the other. That's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me."
While saying his memory was not entirely clear due to his injury, Machchhar said he managed to pull open the cockpit door "but I think he shut it back closed."
"I had that one last fight left in me," Machchhar explained, saying he knew he faced certain death if not.
"That's when I pushed against everything. I gave everything that I had and just went for the door and opened the door and thankfully people were waiting."
bee66e10e188a3ee: PETALING JAYA: An earthquake with a magnitude of 6.0 struck the Sumbawa region of Indonesia at 6.55am today.
Sumbawa is an island located in the middle of the Lesser Sunda Islands chain between Lombok and Flores.
The Malaysian meteorological department (MetMalaysia) said the quake, at a depth of 87km, occurred 140km south of Bima, a city located on the eastern coast of Sumbawa Island.
It said there was no tsunami threat to Malaysia.
e5fe3d8e079faa42: KUALA LUMPUR: Fraudulent motor insurance claims account for an estimated RM1 billion in losses annually, said insurance adjusters.
Association of Malaysian Loss Adjusters (AMLA) chairman Y.K. Foo said the most prevalent fraudulent claims involved accidents, vehicle thefts, fires and staged collisions.
"While the majority of claims submitted to insurers are genuine, fraud remains a persistent issue," he said.
Foo said an adjusting firm could handle an average of 200 suspicious cases requiring formal investigation each year.

"Following thorough inquiries, approximately 40 to 50 per cent of these flagged cases are confirmed as actual, actionable fraud, with overall fraud incidence rates remaining relatively stable year on year."
He said AMLA had 41 members, nearly half of whom dealt with motor insurance fraud, while the rest handled other investigations and insurance claims.
Foo said the scams ranged from opportunistic individual policy breaches to highly organised syndicate operations.
"At the individual level, the most common tactic involves lapsed policies, in which vehicle owners who crash while uninsured quickly purchase a new policy before reporting the accident days later.
"Claims submitted within a week of renewing a long-lapsed policy are immediate red flags for investigators.
"Illegal operators sometimes pair an uninsured, damaged vehicle from a repair yard with an insured vehicle to stage a fake multi-vehicle crash and claim payouts on both.
"Another tactic involves faking or exaggerating personal injuries."
He said fraudsters previously preferred driving vehicles into monsoon drains, lakes or rivers to claim insurance, but a crackdown on those claims had prompted a shift towards vehicle arson.
"With fire, everything is destroyed and little evidence remains, apart from traces of accelerants."
He added that arson incidents had risen to around 20 cases annually per firm.

Foo also warned motorists against accident-scene touts who exploit drivers' panic to initiate fraudulent claims, with unscrupulous operators routinely towing vehicles to unapproved locations to cause secondary damage or re-impact them to inflate claim amounts.

"Everyone will be in a state of shock after an accident and may not know what to do. These unscrupulous people will tow your vehicle somewhere and probably tamper with the damage or bang the car again to inflate the claim amount."
To curb the issue in the long term, AMLA is advocating better information-sharing among insurers, adjusters, law enforcement agencies and medical institutions.

Foo added that if the entire ecosystem could develop a process through which legitimate claim information was shared quickly and securely, industry stakeholders could work together to reduce fraud and, ultimately, keep consumer premiums within a controlled percentage.
43db9ebd50741a63: WASHINGTON: The prison commissioner in the southern US state of Tennessee has resigned over the botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike, governor Bill Lee said Saturday.
Lee said in a statement that commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post this month.
Pike's lawyers say she is in critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator in a hospital, after her execution by lethal injection went wrong on Wednesday.
Pike, 50, survived two injections of the normally lethal substance pentobarbital as punishment for the murder of Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
It was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. The state halted an execution in May after medical staff failed to tap a vein in the prisoner's arm.
Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
In the same statement, Strada said, "I continue to believe the Department (of Correction) carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol."
Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, has halted further executions through the rest of the year while a review is conducted.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state in more than two centuries.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
d1f95244d994ae4a: IN the soft hush of memory, where chalk dust once lingered in the morning light and rows of young faces waited with anticipation, two women look back on lives spent in classrooms — lives neither of them could have fully imagined at the beginning.
For Theresa Loh Kam Toh, now 84, teaching was the career she never intended to choose. "I wanted to be a nurse," she recalls, adding: "Teaching was the last career I would choose."

The thought of standing before a classroom of more than 40 students filled her with dread. During her teacher training, the scrutiny of lecturers observing her every move only deepened her hesitation.
"I told myself, 'No way'," she confides with a small smile, almost amused by the memory.

Yet, while awaiting her Cambridge examination results, Loh was approached by her Secondary Convent principal, Sr Xavier Casey, to "help out" at the primary school. It was actually meant to be temporary.
Instead, it was the beginning of a teaching life that would span decades. "Little did I realise," she says, "that I was actually teaching the little ones."

When the opportunity came to train formally at the I.J. Convent Teachers' College in Bukit Nanas, Kuala Lumpur, she accepted. By 1963, she was standing before her first Form 2 class. A year later, she took on Form 3 students in the morning session.
"Since then, I never looked back," she says softly.
For Repiah Singah, her journey began differently.

For her, teaching was an aspiration that grew into more than three decades of service. She began in 1982 at SM Tengku Mahmud Iskandar in Sungai Mati, Muar, where she taught biology, science and mathematics.
By 1987, she had moved to Institut Pendidikan Guru Temenggong Ibrahim in Johor Baru, where she spent much of her career nurturing not only students but future educators.
When she retired in 2014 at 58 as a senior lecturer and subject specialist in mathematics, she left behind generations of students and teachers who had passed through her care.
Shares the affable 70-year-old: "I aspired to be a versatile, excellent and dedicated teacher. Not just to produce students who excel academically, but those who grow beyond the classroom."
Their classrooms may have been different, their journeys separated by decades, but both women came to understand that teaching was never simply about getting students through examinations.

For Loh, the transformation was something she witnessed over the course of her career. Education, she says, gradually moved away from an emphasis on rote learning and examination results towards a more holistic approach.
Explains Loh: "In the early years, teaching was about facts — about preparing students to pass exams. Today, a teacher is also a mentor, a facilitator and a guide in character building."

For Repiah, the fundamentals remained constant even as the profession became more demanding. "The profession has become more challenging over the years. But what has never changed are the goals and principles of a teacher, namely to educate, guide and to shape character," she says.
And for both these ladies, that responsibility demanded something that could never be measured by a timetable or salary. It was time.
OF SACRIFICES AND PURPOSE

Smiling, Loh recalls that teaching English and mathematics meant endless marking. She taught two classes of English, with essays to be marked every fortnight. She would often remain at her desk during breaks, sandwich in hand, with exercise books piled around her.
Chuckling, she confides: "I hardly went to the canteen. Otherwise, I would have had to take more books home. I guess these were sacrifices I made. But you know what? I have no regrets."

Nodding, Repiah says that she also remembers the same willingness to give more than what was required. "An educator sacrifices time, and often even personal finances, for the sake of students," she says.
The sacrifices, however, were not always visible.

There were students who skipped lessons, struggled to find motivation or simply seemed indifferent to learning. For Repiah, these were not the students to give up on, but the ones who needed more patience, persistence and understanding.

"Such situations must be handled with perseverance," she says, adding: "Success comes when we can rekindle their motivation and remove that sense of laziness. Replace it with purpose instead." Her approach was never about choosing between discipline and compassion.
Both, she believed, had their place in the classroom. Explains Repiah: "One must be firm and punctual, but also constantly guide and motivate. Corrections should be made openly, but constructively."

It is a philosophy that Loh understood equally well. For her, discipline should never come at the expense of a student's dignity. She remembers being deliberate about the way she spoke to children, particularly when they had made mistakes.

"I do not believe in using harsh words because nothing positive comes from it," she says simply. Instead, she chose to listen before judging, believing that empathy and respect could sometimes accomplish what punishment could not.
"A firm but gentle approach works far better," she says.

For Loh, that instinct to understand rather than simply reprimand eventually extended beyond the classroom. In her later years as a school counsellor, she visited students in their homes, taking the time to understand the circumstances behind their behaviour and the struggles they might not have been able to articulate at school.
It was another reminder that, for both women, teaching was never simply about getting a student to learn a lesson. Sometimes, it meant first understanding the person sitting in front of them.
LASTING MEASURE

For Repiah, too, understanding a student was inseparable from teaching one. She believed that a teacher had to look beyond the behaviour in front of them and try to understand what might be driving it.

"Be honest and patient in resolving problems," she advises, adding: "Use psychological approaches to shape character. Stay close to students, especially outside the classroom, and never punish without understanding their mistakes."
Perhaps that is why, when they look back now, it is not the grand achievements they remember most vividly, but the small moments that have stayed with them.
For Loh, one of those memories goes all the way back to her earliest days in the classroom.
She remembers a Standard Six class with particular fondness. "They were angels… so well-behaved and eager to learn," she recalls, the memory still bringing warmth to her voice.

Repiah, meanwhile, remembers the students who initially struggled and the satisfaction of watching them slowly find their footing. For her, few things were more rewarding than seeing weaker students improve, especially when their Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) results finally reflected the effort they and their teachers had put in.
"When their SPM results improved, every effort felt worthwhile," she says softly.
But perhaps the clearest measure of a teacher's influence is only visible years later, when former students return and reveal that something said or taught long ago has stayed with them.

Loh has taught mothers and their daughters, watching generations pass through her classrooms and go on to build lives of their own. Every now and then, however, a former student would return and remind her that some lessons have a way of staying with us.

She recalls meeting two former students who reminded her of advice she had given them years earlier: whatever jobs they eventually took, they should never become "clock-watchers". It was a simple lesson about work ethic, but clearly one that stayed with them long after they had left her classroom.

For Repiah, the clearest sign of her influence came in another form. Some of the students she once taught went on to become teachers themselves, carrying something of her lessons into classrooms of their own.
"I feel grateful, proud and fulfilled," she shares, adding: "… especially when my students go on to become excellent teachers themselves."

Perhaps that is what makes a teacher's influence so difficult to measure. It does not always end with a report card, an examination result or the final school bell. Sometimes, it simply carries on — in the choices former students make, the values they pass on and, for some, the next generation they teach.
FULFILLING JOURNEY
Loh's own teaching journey took an unexpected second turn after she left the teaching service in 1993.

Seven years later, a former student — by then a principal — welcomed her back into education at Tun Dr Ismail International School in Johor Bahru. She later served as director of studies at Sri Ara International School until 2019, finally stepping away from a profession she had once been so reluctant to enter.
But even then, something of the teacher remained. "I still love to teach," she admits.
Perhaps that is why, even in retirement, neither woman speaks of teaching as something that simply ended when they left the classroom.

For Loh, the role of a teacher has only become more demanding in an age of technology and rapid change. Knowledge, she believes, is no longer enough. "It is not about feeding students with knowledge anymore," she says, adding: "It is about helping them think — about developing critical skills and building character."
And if she could offer one message to a new generation of educators, it would be simple. "A teacher does not just impart knowledge. Above all, she inspires."

Meanwhile, Repiah's advice is equally grounded in the values she spent a lifetime trying to instil. "Value time. Be punctual. Follow rules. Cooperate and help one another," she advises. And to young people themselves, she offers a reminder that education should reach beyond academic achievement.
Says Repiah: "Knowledge is important. But beyond that, have self-discipline, respect your teachers, your parents and those around you."
Looking back, neither woman speaks much about the long hours or sacrifices. What remains, instead, is a sense of gratitude for the life they were able to build through their work.
For Loh, the reflection is disarmingly simple. "All I can say is that I enjoyed every moment," she enthuses.
Perhaps that is where these two very different journeys meet.
Loh never planned to become a teacher, while Repiah set out wanting to become one. Yet both found themselves spending decades doing far more than teaching lessons from a textbook.

They taught perseverance, discipline and kindness. They learned to look beyond a student's mistakes and see the person behind them. And, years after the classroom doors have closed, they continue to see traces of that work in the lives of those they once taught.
For a teacher, perhaps there can be no greater measure of a life well spent.
