1eaa078b1da5dc9d: PETALING JAYA: Bekas menteri undang-undang Zaid Ibrahim mempertikaikan jaminan Premier Sarawak Abang Johari Openg bahawa Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (Petros) tidak akan menggantikan atau melemahkan kedudukan Petronas.
Zaid berkata jaminan itu 'tidak selari dengan realiti', sambil merujuk usaha Petros mengambil alih peranan Petronas sebagai agregator gas di Sarawak.
“Petros mahu mengambil alih peranan Petronas sebagai agregator gas. Itu bukan perubahan kecil atau sekadar peranan tambahan.
"Ia bermakna mengambil alih bahagian penting dalam perniagaan Petronas,” katanya di Facebook.
Semalam, Abang Johari berkata peranan Petros yang semakin berkembang dalam sektor gas Sarawak bukan bertujuan menggantikan Petronas.

Beliau berkata Sarawak kekal komited bekerjasama dengan Petronas walaupun pada masa sama meningkatkan keupayaannya sendiri untuk memproses sumber negeri itu, termasuk rancangan membangunkan terminal regasifikasi gas asli cecair (LNG) di Kuching menjelang 2029.

Katanya, Petros sudah lebih setahun mengadakan perbincangan dengan syarikat infrastruktur tenaga Norway, Höegh Evi, dan kedua-dua syarikat mengumumkan perjanjian pembangunan bersama untuk membangunkan, memiliki serta mengendalikan terminal berkenaan.
“Ramai orang kata saya mahu ‘membunuh’ Petronas atau Petros akan melemahkan Petronas. Itu tidak benar. Kita berkongsi peluang dengan Petronas,” katanya seperti dilaporkan.
Bagaimanapun, Zaid berkata tahap kerjasama tidak boleh dinilai berdasarkan jaminan semata-mata, sebaliknya perlu dilihat daripada kesan perubahan yang sedang diusahakan.

Beliau berkata Petronas berpotensi kehilangan berbilion ringgit sekiranya tidak lagi mengawal peranannya sebagai agregator gas di Sarawak, dengan perniagaan gas syarikat itu di negeri berkenaan dianggarkan bernilai kira-kira RM10 bilion setahun.

“Petronas sudah terkesan akibat beberapa tindakan Sarawak. Dalam pertikaian membabitkan Shell, bayaran kira-kira RM80 juta sebulan ditahan ketika timbul kekeliruan mengenai pihak yang sepatutnya menerima bayaran itu,” katanya.

Zaid berkata isu berkenaan bukan sekadar melibatkan urusan komersial kerana Sarawak turut mempersoalkan sama ada Akta Kemajuan Petroleum 1974 (PDA) dan undang-undang petroleum persekutuan lain terpakai di negeri itu.
“Itu bermakna asas perundangan yang menjadi tunjang penubuhan Petronas sendiri sedang dicabar,” katanya.

Beliau memberi amaran sekiranya setiap negeri pengeluar minyak dibenarkan menuntut kawalan sama terhadap sumber petroleum serta bahagian penting dalam rantaian bekalan, ia boleh menjejaskan skala operasi Petronas dan keupayaannya memenuhi kepentingan negara.

“Jika setiap negeri pengeluar minyak melakukan perkara sama, Petronas akan kehilangan skala yang selama ini menjadikannya kukuh. Peranannya di peringkat nasional boleh terjejas dan akhirnya terhakis,” katanya.
Zaid berkata sebarang penyelesaian perlu bermula dengan pengiktirafan jelas terhadap hak Petronas ke atas sumber minyak dan gas Malaysia seperti diperuntukkan di bawah PDA.
“Perkara itu tidak boleh dikompromi. Selepas ia diselesaikan, barulah rundingan boleh dibuat mengenai peranan yang wajar dimainkan Petros dengan mengambil kira keperluan dan keadaan Sarawak.
“Namun, ia tidak boleh bermula dengan Petros mengambil alih fungsi Petronas ketika hak Petronas dari segi undang-undang masih dipertikaikan,” katanya.
5bc78591999e3b4e: ATHENS: Floods after heavy storms trapped some people in their cars and forced the evacuation of some tourists on the Greek holiday island of Crete, local officials said Saturday.
The force of the flooding washed some cars and trees into the sea.
"We had to evacuate a few tourists and a woman had to be taken to hospital as a precaution," the mayor of the Cretan port of Ierapetra, Manolis Frangoulis, told AFP.
The town, on the southeast coast of Crete, was hit by torrential rain Friday and Saturday, cutting off roads that had been filled with debris.
"We have cars in the sea and all the department is working to at least re-establish transport," Frangoulis.
On the road between Ierapetra and Sitia, flooding trapped 23 people in their cars, state television channel ERT reported.
Three tourists and their taxi driver had to abandon their vehicle after flood waters began to carry away their vehicle, ERT added.
At the port of Canea, a popular tourist destination, giant waves damaged seafront restaurants and tourist venues.
The civil protection agency called on residents of several towns to limit their movements.
The deputy governor of the Heraklion region, Nikos Syrigonakis, said emergency services were working to clear small landslides and remove debris from local roads.
They remained on high alert, monitoring the water levels of the streams and rivers, he told the Greek news agency ANA.
Between Friday and Saturday at 1550 GMT (6:50 pm), 42 cm of rain fell in the Canea department, said the Greek national observatory.
The wind speeds were reached up to eight and nine on the Beaufort Scale, said the EMY weather service.
e5a33162cadd6707: PETALING JAYA: Former law minister Zaid Ibrahim has disputed Sarawak premier Abang Johari Openg’s assurance that Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (Petros) will not displace or undermine Petronas.
Zaid said the assurance “does not match reality”, pointing to Petros’s bid to take over Petronas’s role as the gas aggregator in Sarawak.
“Petros wants Petronas’s gas aggregator role. That is not a minor adjustment or a supplementary role. It means taking over a key part of Petronas’s business,” he said on Facebook.
Yesterday, Abang Johari said Petros’s expanding role in Sarawak’s gas sector was not intended to displace Petronas.

He said Sarawak remained committed to working with Petronas while it built up its own ability to process the state’s resources, including plans for a liquefied natural gas regasification terminal in Kuching by 2029.

He said Petros had been in discussions with Norwegian energy infrastructure company Höegh Evi for more than a year, with the two companies announcing a joint development agreement to develop, own and operate the terminal.
“Many people say I want to kill Petronas, or that Petros will undermine Petronas. That is simply not true. We share opportunities with Petronas,” he was quoted as saying.
But Zaid said cooperation could not be judged by assurances alone, but by the effect of the changes being pursued.
He said Petronas stood to lose billions if it lost control of its gas aggregation role in Sarawak, where its gas business is estimated to be worth about RM10 billion a year.
“Petronas has already suffered from Sarawak’s various actions. In the Shell dispute, around RM80 million a month in payments was withheld amid confusion over who should be paid,” he said.
Zaid said the issue went beyond commercial arrangements, as Sarawak was also challenging whether the Petroleum Development Act 1974 and other federal petroleum laws applied in the state.
“That is challenging the very legal foundation on which Petronas was built,” he said.

He warned that allowing individual oil-producing states to assert similar control over petroleum resources and key parts of the supply chain would erode Petronas’s scale and its ability to serve the national interest.
“If every oil-producing state does the same thing, Petronas loses the scale that made it strong. Its national role can be undermined and eventually broken,” he said.
Zaid said the starting point for any settlement must be a clear recognition of Petronas’s rights over Malaysia’s oil and gas resources under the PDA.
“That must be non-negotiable. Once that is settled, then there can be negotiations on the role Petros should play, taking into account Sarawak’s needs and circumstances.
“But it cannot begin with Petros taking over Petronas’s functions while the legal rights of Petronas are still being challenged,” he said.
d834e8743d71b9de: BEIJING: From the audience, Sha Ma Laqian’s high-chair act can look almost effortless. In reality, every controlled movement is backed by 12 years of training, repetition, and the kind of nerve that only comes with experience.
The 19-year-old, a member of China’s Yi ethnic group, began learning acrobatics when he was just seven.
Today, he performs with the Sichuan Suining Acrobatics Troupe, including in a recent Beijing show where he climbed and balanced on a stack of chairs rising about 10m above the stage.
“I was quite nervous when I first started performing this act, but after doing it repeatedly, I no longer feel that way,” he told the media after the performance.
Bernama was among participants of an Asean media programme invited to watch the show, which offered a closer look at how traditional Chinese acrobatics are being presented on contemporary stages.

Laqian said the high-chair routine took years to master, beginning with basic movements before progressing gradually to more difficult skills. It took him around eight to nine years to reach his current level of proficiency.

That process has not been without physical setbacks. "Injuries are common in the field of acrobatics, but the applause and encouragement from the audience make all the effort to learn and improve worthwhile," he shared.

Beyond the technical difficulty, the act carries a theatrical element: his costume incorporates features inspired by the traditional Chinese shusheng style, evoking the image of a classical scholar or student.

The hourlong “Legend of Chinese Charm” show featured more than 60 performers across nine acts, ranging from plate spinning and bowl balancing to bicycle acrobatics, hat juggling and flying motorcycles.
For Laqian, the performance was about more than spectacle. It was also a way to keep refining an art he has loved since childhood, and to share that passion with audiences beyond China.
He hopes each performance will leave more people curious about Chinese acrobatics, and perhaps more appreciative of the skill, discipline and beauty behind it.
babae469f03c5e38: PETALING JAYA: Persoalan mengenai status wakil rakyat PAS yang bertanding atas lambang Barisan Nasional (BN) perlu diselesaikan lebih awal, termasuk implikasi undang-undang apabila hubungan retak.

Penganalisis berkata penggunaan lambang parti sekutu dalam kalangan rakan segabungan bukan 'formula baharu', merujuk kepada penggunaan lambang PAS oleh calon-calon Bersatu di Kelantan pada PRU15, serta calon PH guna lambang PKR pada PRU14.
Namun situasi berpotensi menjadi rumit apabila membabitkan parti daripada gabungan berbeza, dan PAS perlu menjawab sama ada penyandang bertanggungjawab kepadanya atau BN.

"Status keahlian dan implikasi undang-undang antilompat parti perlu dijelaskan dari awal. Jangan tunggu sehingga berlaku perpecahan baru hendak mencari jawapan," kata Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri daripada Global Asia Consulting.
Kelmarin, Timbalan Presiden PAS Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man berkata rundingan pembahagian kerusi dengan Umno pada PRN Melaka sudah mencapai kira-kira 90%.
PAS juga menyatakan kesediaan menggunakan logo BN sekiranya ia dapat membantu memuktamadkan kerjasama berkenaan, seperti disuarakan oleh Presiden Hadi Awang sebelum ini.

PAS yang ketika ini menerajui PN menyatakan kesediaan itu selepas JPPM menggantung semua kegiatan PN susulan aduan Bersatu, yang menurut Bersatu berkenaan pelanggaran perlembagaan PN oleh kepimpinan PN.
Semalam, Umno dilapor mengalu-alukan kesediaan PAS menggunakan lambang BN, namun Naib Presiden Khaled Nordin menekankan keterbukaan itu tidak terpakai kepada semua parti.
"Kenyataan Khaled yang dilihat lebih berhati-hati terhadap penggunaan logo BN oleh parti seperti Wawasan membuka satu lagi persoalan: apakah prinsipnya?" kata Zaharuddin.
Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid dari Universiti Sains Malaysia pula berkata rundingan berkenaan lambang seeloknya antara gabungan.

"Umno dan PAS hanya parti politik, sedangkan BN dan PN adalah gabungan politik yang mana Umno dan PAS merupakan komponen. Rundingan politik eloknya setara: parti dengan parti, gabungan dengan gabungan," katanya.
Beliau berkata Umno tiada alasan untuk menolak komponen PN lain seperti Wawasan, Gerakan dan MIPP jika parti komponen BN lain bersetuju.
78da2c27a68d2460: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 4 — Gone are the days of traditional cinema where it was just about watching movies as audiences today crave more exciting shared experiences.

This change, which can be considered a result of an eventful past six years that included the rise of over-the-top (OTT) platforms coupled with the Covid-19 Pandemic that almost crippled the cinema sector, has also reshaped how audiences view cinemas today.
According to GSC Chief Executive Officer Koh Mei Lee, while audience footfall has shown encouraging signs of recovery, attendance still lags behind pre-pandemic levels by roughly 20 per cent.

“Consumer behaviour has since evolved, with audiences becoming more discerning about entertainment experiences, showing greater demand for premium, immersive and event-driven experiences in cinemas,” Koh said.

GSC is currently Malaysia’s biggest cinema chain operator with a total of 505 screens across 53 locations nationwide, including four ultra-premium ‘Luxe’ locations under its flagship Aurum Theatre and Velvet Cinemas sub-brands.
In an interview with Malay Mail, Koh dived deeper into how they had to revisit the drawing board for their offerings to satisfy this new and growing demand along with other factors leading to it.
Expanding beyond traditional means

In response to the changing landscape of cinema, GSC has expanded its offerings beyond the screen, now shifting to more fan-centric events such as special screenings, concert films, and live viewing parties that come with interactive activities, and of course, freebies.

This can be seen through some of their recent events such as ScareFest 2026, which united horror film enthusiasts with special screenings past midnight, as well as the Football Final Live Viewing Party in conjunction with the recent Fifa World Cup Finals.
They have also introduced out-of-the-box events such as the 24-hour Spider-Man: Brand New Day Marathon, where they offered special showtime slots until 6am.
Their recent Winefest 2026, which focused on food, beverage and lifestyle enthusiasts also demonstrated the versatility of their cinema and dining spaces.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
GSC’s ScareFest 2026 united horror film fans with special screenings past midnight and some ‘uninvited’ guests. — Picture courtesy of GSC

On top of that, GSC has also invested more in premium large-format screens such as IMAX, 4DX and ScreenX to meet current demand. The latest examples can be seen through the introduction of IMAX with Laser halls at GSC Paradigm in Johor as well as in IOI Mall Damansara.
“Audience preferences are constantly evolving, and we see that as an opportunity to redefine what the cinema experience can be.
“Audiences still love watching great movies on the big screen, but they’re also seeking additional social and memorable experiences.

“GSC connects storytelling, technology, lifestyle, community — uniting film, F&B, events and digital experiences all under one brand, and as such we have expanded beyond just traditional movie screenings,” Koh said.

She also said that these experiences actually complement movies even more instead of replacing them, adding that their goal is to keep pushing the boundaries of cinema by creating total entertainment experiences while preserving the magic of the big screens.
Veiled challenges
Koh pointed out that running a cinema chain is not an easy feat and more often than not, its challenges are often overlooked especially when it comes to operating costs.

She shared that operating cinemas involves high fixed overheads — such as technology maintenance, utilities, and staffing — making operational efficiency essential even as attendance lags behind pre-pandemic levels.

This is why policy relief has proven vital, as demonstrated by the government’s decision to reduce the Entertainment Duty in the Federal Territory from 25 per cent to 10 per cent in 2024, which will be in effect until December 2028.

“Box office revenue and cinema screens grew by three per cent and 30 per cent, respectively, contrasting with the broader national trend, which noted declines of 18 per cent in box office revenues and 32 per cent in the number of cinema screens,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
GSC chief executive officer Koh Mei Lee. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin

Koh, who is also part of the local coalition Industry Unite, which is calling for the abolishment of the Entertainments Duty Act 1953, reiterated the importance of its abolishment for the future of the local cinema industry.

“The relief would enable cinema operators like GSC to continue investing in cinema infrastructure, particularly in modernising older locations and upgrading digital technologies across locations to meet the growing demand for premium large-format experiences.
“And also to strengthen the operational resilience of cinemas in an increasingly competitive entertainment landscape,” she said.
Koh also revealed that the growth of OTT or streaming platforms has changed audience behaviour when it comes to opting for cinemas as an entertainment option.
She said that audiences would reserve cinema visits only for major blockbuster and premium large-formats releases such as Obsession, Michael, Toy Story 5, The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
“This makes it increasingly important for GSC to create experiences that cannot be replicated through home entertainment,” she said.
Moving forward

Despite the shifting landscape and veiled challenges, there are still some positive takeaways according to Koh, which include the growing appetite for cinema experiences that extend beyond the ‘movie-verse’.
“We have seen stronger interest in complementary experiences such as themed food and beverage offerings, limited-edition merchandise, fan-centric events, and community gatherings.

“These allow audiences to celebrate their favourite movies together with like-minded fans — creating shared moments and immersive experiences that can only truly come to life within the cinema,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A shot from GSC’s live viewing party of the recent Fifa World Cup Final. — Picture courtesy of GSC

Further supplementing this trend, GSC also offers movie-goers several incentives via their GSC Rewards membership programme and promotions that encourage repeat visits while rewarding movie-goers’ loyalty.

Koh also shared that admissions during the first half of 2025 benefited from a strong line-up of local and Hollywood releases, such as Ne Zha 2, Blood Brothers, Ejen Ali 2 and Captain America: Brave New World.
While the release calendar this year has been more varied, they are expecting a better second half for 2026 with a strong lineup of upcoming blockbusters such as Dune: Part 3 and Avengers: Doomsday.
cfee9ae6effb21bb: Malaysia kerap dijulang di pentas global sebagai model agung masyarakat majmuk yang berjaya. Namun, neraca sebenar citra kenegaraan kita tidak pernah terpahat pada keangkuhan menara kaca dan keluli yang membelah awan, tidak pula pada angka kaku pembangunan fizikal. Sebaliknya, ia bersemayam dalam keheningan jalinan manusiawi—seutas tali persaudaraan yang ditenun erat dan utuh dalam sanubari rakyatnya.

Gagasan 'Bangsa Malaysia'—sebuah identiti nasional inklusif yang mula ditiupkan di bawah panji Wawasan 2020—bukan sekadar utopia di atas kertas atau retorik politik yang gersang. Ia adalah nafas yang hidup. Ia merupakan sulaman harian penuh ihsan, toleransi, dan solidariti yang mengalir tenang melintasi tembok kaum serta agama tanpa sebarang kekangan. Paling utama, kemuncak manifestasi identiti ini bukan sekadar disaksikan tatkala kita bersorak meraikan puncak kejayaan, tetapi lebih terserlah ketika kita berdiri bahu-membahu menanggung badai duka nasional yang mendalam.

Keindahan yang meruntun jiwa ini terpancar dalam suasana pilu yang menyelubungi upacara keberangkatan pulang ke Rahmatullah, Dr Hasmah Ali. Dalam detik kesedihan yang mencengkam itu, saripati 'Bangsa Malaysia' hadir sewajarnya. Di sana, mengelilingi dan menongkat rapuhnya bekas perdana menteri Dr Mahathir Mohamad, berdiri teguh sebuah pasukan barisan hadapan pelbagai kaum: seorang doktor Melayu, seorang jururawat India, dan seorang pakar fisioterapi Cina.

Kehadiran mereka pada babak terakhir kehidupan seorang ikon negara ini bukan sekadar pelunasan tugas profesional. Ia adalah simbolik akrab tentang ikatan kekeluargaan merentas budaya yang subur membisu dalam masyarakat kita—satu terjemahan hidup bagi pesanan leluhur, bagai aur dengan tebing, yang menggambarkan betapa kita saling berpaut dan melengkapi. Pemergian sosok yang disayangi ini berjaya menzahirkan apa yang sering kali gagal digapai oleh percaturan politik: ia menyatukan rakyat daripada pelbagai rencam ras, agama, dan latar belakang dalam satu acuan duka serta penghormatan terakhir yang syahdu.

Detik-detik yang merenggut emosi ini membuktikan secara mutlak bahawa di sebalik kepelbagaian warna kulit, budaya, dan hamparan iman, rakyat negara ini pada hakikatnya diikat oleh takdir kemanusiaan yang serupa. Ia menghidupkan kembali pesanan keramat—cubit paha kanan, paha kiri terasa juga—bahawa apabila seorang daripada kita terluka, pedihnya mencucuk ke seluruh pelosok jiwa kita semua.
Air mata tidak mengenal warna kulit

Melusuri sejarah, benteng keharmonian yang utuh ini sebenarnya dibina daripada abu runtuhan detik tergelap kita. Bangkit daripada parut tragedi 13 Mei 1969, negara memahat Rukun Negara pada tahun 1970. Prinsip sakral seperti 'Kesopanan dan Kesusilaan' telah sekian lama menjadi kompas moral yang menuntun arah kita. Menerusi tadbir urus moden, iltizam ini diperkukuh melalui Dasar Perpaduan Negara (DPN) yang berteraskan tunjang 'perpaduan dalam kepelbagaian'. Melalui kerangka ini, kita mengamini sepotong hakikat: kepelbagaian etnik bukanlah retakan yang menanti masa untuk memecahbelahkan watan, sebaliknya ia adalah kepingan mozek dinamik yang membentuk satu potret kesatuan yang indah dan utuh.

Apabila tragedi melanda, tembok pemisah buatan yang sering kali diperbesarkan oleh golongan oportunis akan runtuh dengan sendirinya, digantikan dengan jambatan empati yang kukuh. Air mata tidak pernah mengenal warna kulit; ia adalah tangisan kasih sayang tulen daripada warganegara yang berkongsi tanah air yang sama. Keharmonian organik inilah nadi sebenar yang meniupkan nyawa kepada Malaysia untuk terus berdiri sebagai sebuah negara berdaulat.

Memugar agenda 'Bangsa Malaysia' menuntut lebih daripada sekadar persetujuan yang membisu. Ia mendesak setiap anak watan untuk terus menyemai benih persefahaman, menjunjung tinggi sejarah bersama, dan mempertahankan perpaduan nasional secara aktif. Hanya dengan cara itu Malaysia dapat terus mekar sebagai sebuah negara yang bersatu padu, harmoni, dan benar-benar makmur.

Pada akhirnya, detik-detik perkongsian duka ini hadir sebagai sebuah amaran keras lagi mendesak kepada para politikus dan seluruh lapisan masyarakat. Kekuatan, kestabilan, dan maruah masa depan Malaysia tidak boleh digadaikan pada sentimen politik toksik yang memecahbelahkan, yang mampu meruntuhkan sendi masyarakat kita dalam sekelip mata. Kerana kemajuan sejati, hanya akan lahir daripada muafakat dan persefahaman yang luhur.

c3c7ab32888f00eb: From Moaz Nair
Malaysia is routinely paraded on the global stage as the quintessential model of a successful multicultural society.
But the true measure of nationhood has never been found in the glass and steel of skyscrapers piercing the clouds, nor in the sterile metrics of physical development.
It resides, instead, in the quiet, resilient tapestry of human connections woven between people.
The concept of “Bangsa Malaysia” — an inclusive national identity first conceptualised under the ambitious banner of Wawasan 2020 — is far from a mere paper-thin ideal or empty political rhetoric.
It is a lived, breathing reality. It is a daily practice of compassion, tolerance, and solidarity that effortlessly transcends ethnic and religious divides.
Crucially, the truest manifestation of this identity is not witnessed when we are cheering in collective triumph, but when we stand shoulder-to-shoulder in moments of profound, national grief.
We saw this beautifully, and heartbreakingly, in the sombre atmosphere surrounding Dr Hasmah Ali’s funeral.

In a moment of deep sorrow, the essence of “Bangsa Malaysia” was vividly on display. There, surrounding and supporting former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad, was a multi-ethnic frontline team: a Malay doctor, an Indian nurse, and a Chinese physiotherapist.

Their presence during the final chapters of a national icon’s life was not merely an exercise in professional duty. It was a profound symbol of the cross-cultural, familial bonds that thrive quietly in our communities — a living embodiment of the classic Malay proverb “bagai aur dengan tebing”, illustrating how we rely on and complement one another.
The passing of a revered figure did what politics so often fails to do: it united citizens across races, religions, and backgrounds in a collective expression of grief and final respect.

Such poignant moments demonstrate that beneath the diversity of our skin tones, cultural practices, and faiths, the people of this country are fundamentally bound by a shared humanity. It evokes the powerful sentiment that when one of us hurts, we all feel the pain.
Tears bear no racial colours
Historically, this fragile fortress of harmony was built from the ashes of our darkest hours.
Rising from the tragedy of May 13, 1969, the nation introduced the Rukun Negara in 1970. Principles such as “Courtesy and Morality” have long served as our collective moral compass.
In modern governance, this commitment is reinforced through the National Unity Policy, which centres on “Unity in Diversity”.
Through this framework, we acknowledge a vital truth: our ethnic diversity is not a fracture waiting to shatter the nation, but a vibrant mosaic forming a beautiful, cohesive whole.
When tragedy strikes, the artificial walls of division that are so often amplified by opportunists naturally crumble, replaced by bridges of empathy.

Tears bear no racial colours; they are a genuine manifestation of the love shared among citizens who also share a common homeland. This organic harmony is the true heartbeat sustaining Malaysia as a sovereign nation.

Championing the “Bangsa Malaysia” agenda requires more than just passive agreement. It demands that every citizen continuously nurture the seeds of mutual understanding, honour our shared history, and actively uphold national unity.
Only then can Malaysia continue to flourish as a united, harmonious, and truly prosperous nation.
Ultimately, these moments of shared grief serve as a powerful, urgent reminder to politicians and all segments of society.
Malaysia’s future strength, stability, and progress cannot rely on the toxic, divisive political sentiments that threaten to dismantle our social fabrics overnight.
Progress is born from consensus and mutual understanding.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

eedf5efd5c2a9331: JASIN: Among Maimunah Kaus’s cherished photographs is one taken at her wedding to Othman Ismail in August 1967. Another brings together three generations of her family: her husband wearing his medals, their son Ahmad Azani, and their grandson Yusof Ahmad Azani, a Royal Malaysian Navy lieutenant.
To the nation, Othman was a decorated soldier who served through years of the communist insurgency. To Maimunah, he was the caring companion with whom she raised three daughters and two sons.
“He was a very caring family man who nurtured his children to become successful model citizens,” she said.

Othman, a retired staff sergeant and recipient of the Panglima Gagah Berani (PGB) award, died of heart complications at his Taman Kolam Air home on Sept 7. He was 82 and had experienced declining health in recent years.

His death recently brought fellow veterans to the family’s side. Members of the SP/PGB/PTU Club, which brings together military recipients of three gallantry awards, pooled their contributions to offer Maimunah some support.
Club president Hanafiah Ali, a retired major, and patron Abdul Rahim Abdul Rahman, a retired brigadier-general, visited her home to present RM2,000. Both men, themselves PGB recipients, are 79.
Joining them were Hanafiah’s wife Zawiyah Othman and daughter Diana Farhana, along with Othman’s son Abdul Aziz, and granddaughters Nur Anis Natasha and Nur Ayu Amira.

The visit was part of the club's commitment to remain present in the lives of its members and their families. “We will keep tabs on her wellbeing, just as we do for the living warrior members of our club,” Rahim said.

In one of his last interviews, Othman recalled joining the army on May 20, 1965. He served with the Royal Malay Regiment until his retirement in 1987, having chosen a military career partly because of the fear and disruption his family and friends had experienced during the insurgency.
“I had decided after school that I wanted to do my part for the nation to eradicate the insurgency threat,” he said.
His service included the Second Emergency from 1968 to 1989. Of the operations in which he took part, one encounter in Pahang remained particularly vivid.

In October 1974, Othman was a corporal leading a small team during Ops Indera IV at the Samling rubber plantation near Sungai Ruai in Raub. They were returning to their post when they encountered insurgents at sunset.
“I was leading my small team as a corporal then. On the way back to our post after conducting counter-insurgency operations, we stumbled upon several insurgents who fired at us,” he recalled.
The four soldiers exchanged fire. Othman shot an insurgent who was attempting to throw a hand grenade at his team, before his company commander arrived with reinforcements.
“We secured the area overnight and recovered the insurgents’ bodies the next day to be brought to our main post,” he added.
Othman's actions led to a recommendation for the PGB, the country’s second-highest gallantry award after the Seri Pahlawan Gagah Perkasa (SP).
Looking back, Othman also spoke about the everyday demands of service: loyalty, discipline, following instructions, and doing one's best.
“There was no tolerance for indiscipline and insubordination,” he said. “It inculcated in me a sense of patriotism and to appreciate the freedom and peace we enjoy today.”
Memories across generations

At home, Maimunah remembers a devoted husband and father whose concern for his children continued long after his military career ended. She now lives with Abdul Aziz, 56, a security guard at Jasin Hospital.

The family portrait of Othman with his son and grandson was Ahmad Azani’s idea. A lecturer at UiTM Shah Alam, he had arranged for his father to be photographed in his medal-decked jacket alongside himself and Yusof in naval uniform.
For Maimunah, it is a treasured image of the family they built together. Beside the wedding photograph, it records how much changed over nearly six decades of marriage.
According to the veterans' club, 32 members survive from its roll of 107 military recipients of the SP, PGB and Pingat Tentera Udara awards.
Rahim said Othman’s RM1,500 monthly PGB allowance would cease following his death, although Maimunah would be eligible for a RM1,300 monthly derivative pension and benefits including healthcare.
He expressed hope that the club's donation would help ease her financial burden.

For the family, Othman’s medals and photographs preserve different sides of the man they loved, while his comrades’ promise to keep looking out for Maimunah offers another form of remembrance - one marked by visits, contributions and kindness.

10cb2647cf5631e8: The second Anthropic-linked vulnerability known to have been exploited in the wild saw initial activity from an IP address in China targeting vulnerable hosts in the US and Japan. The vuln is a critical authentication-bypass bug in Rejetto HTTP File Server (HFS) that can lead to full admin access and remote code execution. HFS is an open source web file server that previously appeared on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities in 2024. On Wednesday, researcher Zach Hanley at AI pen-testing company Horizon3 said he used Mythos to uncover a new flaw in the file server, now tracked as CVE-2026-61500. If you use Rejetto HFS, be sure to update to v3.2.1 or later, which fixes this and other security flaws. Hanley also published a video showing the steps to exploit HFS and remotely execute code on the server. By the next day, the CVE was under exploitation. “We started detecting exploitation of CVE-2026-61500 in Rejetto HFS this evening,” VulnCheck security researcher Patrick Garrity posted on LinkedIn on Thursday, adding that Hanley and team reported the bug to VulnCheck for CVE assignment. “Our canaries detected an actor in China targeting real vulnerable hosts in the US,” Garrity added. Garrity has been tracking CVEs attributed to Mythos and Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s initiative to give select partners access to the bug-hunting model, since shortly after the program was announced in April. Anthropic claims that Mythos is too powerful to release to the general public (insert evil laugh). As of Friday, Mythos and Project Glasswing have uncovered 286 CVEs, according to Garrity’s tracker, and up until Thursday only one of these bugs had been exploited in real-world attacks. The Thursday night activity originated from one IP address in China and targeted vulnerable servers in the US and Japan, Garrity told The Register. “Today we have seen four hits,” he told us on Friday. These originated from two different IP addresses in the US: 173.239.211[.]248 and 173.239.211[.]249. Both are in the same subnet, and “appear to be coming from a proxy,” Garrity added. China-linked digital intruders routinely use compromised devices as proxies to route malicious traffic and disguise the attackers’ true location, and in April a 10-country security advisory warned of China-nexus cyber operatives using proxy networks “strategically, and at scale.” In his write-up, Hanley said Horizon3 has used Mythos in its vulnerability research – and discovered “many critical vulnerabilities” – ever since the security company joined Project Glasswing in July. Mythos' mad math skillz CVE-2026-61500 highlights a couple of Mythos capabilities that make it really good at uncovering vulnerabilities, according to Hanley. Namely, Mythos excels at mathematical distillations and scientific tasks, especially those relating to computer science and operating systems. Finding this CVE “speaks to Mythos’s capabilities in understanding of mathematics, how it identified an exploitable set of cryptographic missteps, and approached solving the constraints to achieve remote code execution,” Hanley wrote. The security issue stems from how HFS authenticates users. It generates a random value with Math.random() and then passes this value to Koa, the Node.js web framework foundation for HFS. Koa uses keygrip to sign all session cookies with that random value. This means that if an “attacker can derive what the session signing key is, they can forge valid session cookies,” Hanley said. This should not be possible, assuming Math.random() uses a secure pseudo random number generator (PRNG). But V8’s Math.random() did not use a secure PRNG. Mythos discovered that the output of the xorshift128+ algorithm it used was fully reversible – and the application was leaking Math.random() outputs. The model’s analysis claimed that Z3, a Microsoft-developed, publicly available Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solver, could be used to recover the PRNG seed. Hanley notes that Horizon3’s researchers could not recall seeing an SMT solver used this way to attack a cryptographic flaw in a real application and bypass authentication. “What makes this impressive is that Mythos didn’t just flag the insecure PRNG in isolation – it simultaneously identified that the application leaked raw Math.random() outputs through a separate code path, recognized those two facts as a chain, and determined the leak produced exactly the observations needed to make state recovery feasible,” he wrote.®

89f7165e2ebfe859: "Can it run Doom?" now applies to databases, as the author of DOOMQL has released a far more visually accurate port. There's a saying: "Be careful what you wish for." In 2025, we wrote a piece about a database boffin coming up with a version of Doom that was written in SQL. It was neat, but the visuals were nearer to 3D Monster Maze than to the 90s pixel blaster. We commented, "If persuading SQL to do the entire rendering pipeline is a 'bad idea,' we cannot wait for a terrible one." And so here we are. The author, Lukas Vogel, has been at it again and ported both Doom's game logic and renderer to SQL, running it in a database. Python handles timing, keyboard input, and bitmap display, but the rest comes from SQL queries and the CedarDB database. DOOMQL was an undeniably impressive thing. However, Vogel told The Register, "Someone on Hacker News complained last year when I did the first iteration that that one was more Wolfenstein-like because I used raycasting instead of BSP-tree traversal which was *the thing* that made Doom revolutionary. "So I obviously couldn't let that stand." Which brings us to SQLDoom. Doom, ported to SQL. In his blog, Vogel noted the ground rules for the port. Unlike DOOMQL, this had to look like real Doom. The rendering had to be purely SQL-based: "the only acceptable SQL output is a table or a bitmap encoding exact RGB values for every pixel," and the game loop also had to be purely SQL-based. Vogel told us, "I was very thrilled to find out that porting the real Doom was a) feasible and b) the performance was actually *better* than the much more barebones approach from last year! "Also, at some point I started actually playing it for fun in my free time, which is still a very strange feeling. I intended it as a tech demo, but it just feels like the real Doom, even though it doesn't share a single line of code with any existing Doom port. So I wanted to see how far I could take it. "In the end, I even got deathmatch to work." According to Vogel, the game is perfectly playable on his laptop (using a Ryzen 7 7840U), and multiplayer games can be played online using EU and US servers. We found the server performance a little sluggish – likely more due to the servers than the port – although getting SQL to jump through these hoops is something that, only a few short years ago, would be unimaginable. It's worth keeping in mind that this is a thinly veiled demonstration of the capabilities of CedarDB. It's a compiling database system where complex queries are eventually compiled to machine code. Still, it's hard not to get swept up in Vogel's enthusiasm and the fact that this is Doom… running in a database. Certainly this is a lot more fun than recreating yet another online store for yet another interminable keynote. ®

5014b38aa281e81d: “I always laugh at the IT industry’s terms,” says Ryan Sheehan, a senior vice president at $16 billion global solutions integrator SHI. And right now the jargon that gets him giggling is “forward-deployed engineer” (FDE) because, as he told The Register at VMware's September Explore conference, “We have been doing FDE for a long time.” “Doing FDE” involves sending top consultants to a client, without tying them to a project. Instead they get a mission to build something valuable using new technology, and carte blanche to make that happen in a hurry. Sheehan has company in believing FDEs aren’t fundamentally new. Cloud monitoring vendor DoIT told The Register it has used FDEs since 2011, but only started using the term in the last quarter of 2025, when it changed the name of its “Customer Reliability Engineering” practice to FDE. That decision came as services companies adopted the term FDE to describe the work needed to build AI proofs of concept. The name has its origins at Palantir, whose chief technology officer Shyam Sankar claims he coined it in 2007 after a conversation in which his CEO Alex Karp asked him why French restaurants are so good. Karp apparently answered his own question by saying, “The wait staff is actually part of the kitchen staff. They intimately understand the food, the methodology, and the technique. They are not merely carrying the food from the kitchen to the table, but are instead part of a subtle and complex system that affects kitchen operations.” Sankar says Karp asked him “to build that, but for engineering” so he did and called it “forward deployed engineering.” “FDEs embed alongside our customers and work to ensure our software solves their problem and not some proxy for their problem,” Sankar wrote on his personal Substack. “They’re crazy enough to get on a last-minute plane to Iraq, they’re smart enough to ship quality, same-day code, and their EQ is still high enough to talk to users (and maybe even enjoy it).” Sankar says Palantir’s investors thought FDEs were a bad idea because the costs they incurred ate into margins, but says they’re worth it because they ensure customers understand the company’s products and how to get value from them. “We didn’t believe in throwing our software over the wall in the hopes the customer would divine the correct meaning from it,” Shankar wrote. “This approach built an engineering organization with unmatched creativity, responsiveness, and focus on the primacy of winning.” AWS likes winning, too, and in June announced a dedicated AWS FDE organization, and $1 billion to fund it. In July Microsoft trumped that with a $2.5 billion so-called “Frontier Company” it claims “goes beyond” FDEs. Both companies see FDEs as a way to get their consultants into customers to help them build AI apps. They argue FDEs’ time has come because, as Palantir found when users struggled to put its software to work, organizations often struggle to turn AI experiments into production applications. Stop us if you've heard this one before But vendors also admit that FDEs aren’t entirely new. Indeed, AWS told The Register it has offered customers something very similar to an FDE for years. “We started this journey all the way back in 2017 when the focus was machine learning (ML),” said Taimur Rashid, the cloud giant’s managing director for go to market, Frontier AI Engineering & Services. “We created a team called the ML Solutions Lab. The idea was that the tech is new, customers need to navigate it. So we said ‘Why don’t we loan them a data scientist?’ They can build a PoC, and the customer can build on our platform.” Rashid says AWS sometimes called this sort of arrangement a “secondment,” a “resident architect” or a “resident scientist.” Whatever you call it, Rashid said the approach worked well so AWS decided to evolve it when generative AI burst onto the scene – this time using an applied scientist and a strategist, and an evolved approach. “We forward-deploy them – they will help to identify the art of the possible and develop the solution for you or with you,” Rashid explained. “They will be part of your business and operational workflows, and effectively be yours for a defined time,” he said. That’s different to conventional services engagements, he argues, because there’s no scope of work, no hourly charge for consultants’ services. “What is different about FDE is you are saying the customer wants to build. The path is not determined.” Carlos Pereira, a Fellow and Chief Architect in Cisco’s Customer Experience team, also admited FDEs aren’t entirely new, but argued AI makes them more valuable than conventional consultants. "The idea of an expert being embedded on-site to help a customer adopt new technology and solutions isn't new,” he told The Register by email. “Our Customer Success organization has been doing this for years.” “The evolution is that AI is now a key part of that equation,” he added. “It introduces new variables like non-deterministic AI models, evaluations, faster-moving requirements, and specialized skills that not every customer team has in-house.” Analyst firms Gartner and Forrester agree that FDEs can be useful, and that this form of IT services differs due to greater intimacy between client and consultant. “They often have full-stack access to the customer’s environment and the vendor’s codebase, allowing them to build and iterate in real time,” Gartner’s Arun Chandrasekaran and Robert Thanaraj wrote in March guidance titled “An AI Leader’s Guide to Forward Deployed Engineering to Scale AI.” A June best practice report from five Forrester analysts, titled “Forward-Deployed Engineers: Use provider-embedded builders to improve outcomes,” praises the model for helping to “accelerate adoption and turn complex platforms into production-ready outcomes.” Yet both analyst firms also warn that using FDEs may see clients develop a dependency on the vendor that provides them. “The allure of delivering outcomes at speed can induce blind spots and is fraught with risks,” according to Forrester. “Without the appropriate guardrails on tech architecture and stack choices, teams can fall into a bespoke trap, where highly tailored solutions deepen vendor dependence and make future change costly.” Debt and dependency Gartner urges would-be hirers of FDEs to “beware of ill-conceived FDE engagements that can lead to a high degree of vendor dependency, security/data risk exposure, technical debt, and talent atrophy.” The latter happens when organizations hire FDEs but don’t train their own teams on new tech. “Your internal team may become operators of a black box rather than architects, making it difficult to innovate without the vendor,” Gartner warns. Gartner also worries FDEs can be a fast-track to technical debt. “A major concern with the FDE model is that it relies heavily on manually designed structures and hard-coded domain knowledge. Such human-engineered components tend to deliver short-term gains but are repeatedly superseded as more general, scalable learning systems improve.” “As large language models continue to advance, much of this manually encoded logic is likely to be rendered obsolete, requiring costly rework or full redesign, and creating a long-term technical and organizational burden.” FDEs themselves may soon be obsolete, because they’re not vendors’ only bet on improving AI consultancy skills, according to Omdia chief analyst Jay McBain. “At the same time as investing in FDEs, the big players have been investing big into partner enablement,” he told The Register. “They are playing both ends.” The tech services channel doesn’t mind that, because according to Omdia data 82 percent of partners report they “aren’t ready” to quickly grow their AI services. The vendors promoting FDEs, meanwhile, don’t want to use this form of consultancy for long. “None of these companies’ investors want to dilute a low-value services business into the overall revenue,” McBain wrote. “We are predicting all of this FDE investment will fall back into the channel by 2031 when this matures.” Which rather suggests that in a few years we’ll all be laughing at how Palantir re-heated an old form of tech services under a new name, and the rest of the industry decided to follow the same recipe. ®

c6df0ba4697c2ff2: Pearly Tan-M Thinaah did their job.
They fought their way into the Asian Games semi-finals, pushed the world No 1 Chinese pair hard and brought home Malaysia’s only badminton medal from Aichi-Nagoya.
It was a bronze, and Malaysia’s first women’s doubles medal at the Games in 12 years. Pearly and Thinaah deserve every bit of credit.
But one pair on the podium cannot disguise what happened around them.

Malaysia’s men’s singles players were gone by the last 16. Aaron Chia-Tee Kai Wun fell in the same round, while Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani went out in the quarter-finals. Neither mixed doubles combination reached the last eight.
For a badminton nation with Malaysia’s resources, depth and expectations, this should prompt more than another round of post-tournament analysis.
Has Malaysian badminton become jaded? And, somewhere amid the reshuffles, reviews and long-term plans, has the Badminton Association of Malaysia (BAM) lost the plot?
The problem is not a lack of talent. Malaysia has players capable of beating the best. The frustration is how often that potential appears in flashes without becoming sustained performance.
The men’s doubles situation offers a telling example.
Aaron Chia and Soh Wooi Yik were split, with Aaron paired with Tee Kai Wun. BAM has presented the changes as part of its longer-term planning towards the 2028 Olympics.
That is a legitimate objective but long-term planning cannot become a convenient shelter for every short-term disappointment.
Experiments must produce evidence. New pairings need a clear purpose, and players must know what they are building towards. Otherwise, movement starts to look like direction.
Razif Sidek, one of Malaysia’s great doubles players, has warned about the risks of major changes before a big tournament.
He felt the reshuffling affected seeding and exposed Malaysia to difficult opponents early. He also backed Aaron and Tee, while acknowledging that they remain some distance behind the leading pairs.
The issue is not whether BAM should experiment. It should. The issue is whether it knows when an experiment has yielded enough information to stop.
The national and independent systems cannot be treated as separate planets. Players move between them. Some train outside BAM but still represent Malaysia; others return to the national setup.
That fluidity can be an asset, provided the pathway makes sense. BAM should be able to explain how talent is identified, developed, paired, tested and promoted, regardless of where a player trains.
Too much of the conversation, however, revolves around the latest combination rather than the larger plan.
Then there is Nova Widianto.

The Indonesian left BAM at the end of July after more than three years in charge of the mixed doubles programme. His most significant achievement was guiding Chen Tang Jie and Toh Ee Wei to Malaysia’s first mixed doubles world title in 2025.
BAM thanked him for his contribution but did not disclose why he left. By early September, it had yet to finalise his replacement.
At Aichi-Nagoya, Tang Jie partnered Cheng Su Yin, while Goh Soon Huat and Shevon Lai formed Malaysia’s other mixed doubles combination. Neither reached the quarter-finals.
There is no evidence that Nova’s departure caused those results. It would be simplistic to claim otherwise but the timing deserves scrutiny.
Back with Indonesia, Nova guided Amri Syahnawi and Nita Violina Marwah to the Asian Games final, where they won silver.

That does not prove BAM made the wrong decision in allowing him to leave. It does raise a more pertinent question: did the association have a succession plan before one of its most successful recent coaches departed?
The questions extend beyond the coaching bench. They reach the leadership itself.

BAM president Tengku Zafrul Aziz has put forward Tangkis 2030 as a roadmap for Malaysian badminton and appointed Lee Chong Wei to chair the Performance Committee. Zafrul has chosen not to chair a committee himself, citing the need to avoid conflicts of interest.
That is a matter of structure, not an escape from responsibility.

A president need not dictate coaching tactics or choose a doubles partner. But he must ensure that the people entrusted with those decisions are working towards clear targets, that their performance is reviewed and that shortcomings lead to action.
What does Zafrul regard as measurable progress under Tangkis 2030? When does he decide that a strategy is not working? And who must answer when it fails to deliver?
Lee’s stature in Malaysian badminton is beyond argument. His record as a player makes him one of the sport’s defining figures in this country.
But being a great player and managing high-performance sport are different jobs.

Lee has chaired BAM’s Performance Committee since October 2025. The committee works with the coaching and player-development structure on performance. That makes its work a legitimate subject for examination.

After nearly a year, what has actually changed under Lee’s chairmanship? What evidence supports the decisions to alter pairings? How does the committee measure progress, and what happens when targets are missed?
These are questions about Lee the administrator, not Lee the legend.
The same scrutiny must apply to the singles programme.
Kenneth Jonassen took charge of the men’s singles only in January 2025. It would be unfair to lay a decade of disappointment at the feet of a coach who has been in the job for less than two years.
But Malaysia cannot keep talking about the future without defining when it is expected to arrive.
Both singles programmes need a serious review of tactics, consistency, preparation and player development. Not another promise that the next generation will come good.
China is no longer the only benchmark
The wider Asian badminton landscape is changing. China remains formidable, but it no longer sets the entire rhythm of the sport.
Indonesia, Korea, Japan, India, Thailand and others have developed players and combinations capable of challenging the established order.
That should create opportunities for Malaysia. Instead, it makes the lack of clarity harder to excuse.
If the gap at the top is narrowing, BAM should be identifying where Malaysia can close it. It cannot do so by endlessly rearranging the furniture.
Aichi-Nagoya must be treated as more than a medal tally.

Malaysia has the talent, experience and institutional knowledge to expect more. What it needs is a clear connection between them, backed by decisions that can be measured and leaders prepared to answer for the results.
The danger is not one unsatisfactory tournament. It is becoming too accustomed to explaining why the next one will be different.
At some point, explanations become a substitute for progress, and Malaysian badminton cannot afford to mistake the two.

3accee4374e9bdc8: From P Sundramoorthy

The current debate over house arrest has opened an important conversation about the future of Malaysia’s criminal justice system. The immediate issue concerns the legal basis, eligibility, safeguards and judicial oversight of house arrest.

But from a criminological perspective, the bigger question is whether Malaysia has a sufficiently integrated mechanism to continuously examine emerging challenges across policing, prosecution, courts, corrections, rehabilitation and crime prevention.

Malaysia does not currently have a dedicated statutory framework comprehensively governing house arrest. Recent reporting has highlighted questions concerning the legal basis, implementation, monitoring, restrictions and accountability surrounding such arrangements.

A constitutional lawyer has described the situation as entering relatively “uncharted” legal territory, while a December 2025 High Court decision raised questions about whether an existing legal provision could be used to implement house arrest in the absence of specific legislation.

This does not mean that house arrest itself is necessarily inappropriate. Modern correctional systems in several jurisdictions use forms of home detention, parole, electronic monitoring and supervised community release.

Malaysia itself has operated a parole system since 2008, with the Parole Board required to consider matters including public safety, the nature of the offence, criminal history, risk of reoffending, reintegration and the impact on victims.
The lesson is that alternatives to imprisonment require clear legislation, transparent criteria, professional risk assessment, supervision and accountability.
The central criminological concern, therefore, should be system design rather than personalities.

Any future house-arrest legislation should clearly establish eligibility, exclusions, risk assessment, electronic monitoring, breach procedures, judicial oversight, victims’ interests, review mechanisms and reporting requirements. It should also clearly distinguish between administrative discretion, correctional management, judicial sentencing and constitutional clemency.
Without such clarity, different institutions may interpret their respective powers differently, creating uncertainty and potentially undermining public confidence.
However, house arrest is only one example of a much larger problem. Malaysia's criminal justice system is confronting increasingly complex challenges.

Organised crime is becoming more transnational; cybercrime and technology-enabled fraud are expanding; artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities for both criminals and law enforcement; drug trafficking networks continue to evolve; financial crime increasingly exploits social engineering; youth offending presents changing patterns; and prisons face continuing challenges involving overcrowding, rehabilitation, illicit activity and reintegration.

These problems cannot be examined exclusively through the perspective of one institution. A police response alone cannot solve organised crime. Prison expansion alone cannot solve recidivism. Longer sentences alone cannot necessarily reduce offending. Public awareness alone cannot adequately address sophisticated financial scams.
Likewise, new laws introduced in response to individual controversies may create unintended consequences if their wider criminological and operational implications are not assessed beforehand.
This is why I have, on several occasions, proposed the establishment of a Criminal Justice Advisory Commission for Malaysia.

Such a commission should not replace the courts, Parliament, the police, the Attorney-General's Chambers, the prisons department or existing oversight bodies. Rather, it should provide an independent, multidisciplinary and evidence-based mechanism to examine the criminal justice system across institutional boundaries.

Its mandate could include reviewing crime trends, policing strategies, prosecution and case-management issues, sentencing policy, prison population and overcrowding, parole and community corrections, rehabilitation, recidivism, victim protection, juvenile offending, organised and transnational crime, cybercrime, corruption risks and emerging technologies.
It should also examine whether laws introduced for one purpose are producing unintended consequences elsewhere in the system.
International examples of system-wide coordination

England and Wales have a Criminal Justice Board bringing together senior leaders from policing, prosecution, courts, prisons, probation and other justice institutions to maintain oversight and promote collaboration.

New Zealand has a Justice Sector Leadership Board providing shared direction across six core justice agencies, supported by a dedicated directorate for system-wide coordination. New Zealand has also used independent advisory groups to facilitate wider public discussion and evidence-based criminal justice reform.
Proposed model
Malaysia should consider a model appropriate to its own constitutional and institutional circumstances.

The proposed commission should ideally comprise criminologists, scholars, former and serving practitioners, legal experts, corrections specialists, psychologists, victim representatives, data and technology experts and civil society representatives. Its membership should be professionally credible and sufficiently independent to provide frank advice, including advice that may be inconvenient to government or individual institutions.

Importantly, the commission should be evidence-driven rather than politically driven. It should have access, subject to appropriate confidentiality and privacy safeguards, to reliable data from the police, prosecution service, courts and corrections system.

Malaysia needs better integration of criminal justice data so that policymakers can see the entire journey from reported crime and investigation through prosecution, conviction, sentencing, imprisonment, parole, rehabilitation and reoffending.

For example, instead of asking only how many crimes are reported, policymakers should also examine detection rates, charging decisions, conviction outcomes, sentence patterns, prison admissions, time served, parole outcomes and recidivism. Such information would enable criminal justice policy to be evaluated according to measurable outcomes rather than public perception alone.
Reporting

The commission should publish regular reports to Parliament, perhaps at least twice a year, identifying emerging risks, evaluating existing policies and proposing reforms. The government should be required to respond formally to major recommendations, while retaining the constitutional and democratic authority to accept, modify or reject them.

This would complement, rather than duplicate, existing oversight mechanisms. Malaysia already has institutions such as the Independent Police Conduct Commission, whose statutory functions include investigating police misconduct and reporting annually to Parliament. The proposed commission would operate at a different level: looking principally at the criminal justice system as an interconnected whole.
A modern criminal justice system cannot afford to operate primarily in reaction to crises. It needs foresight, reliable data, independent expertise and continuous evaluation.
Malaysia has invested considerably in policing, prosecution, courts and corrections. The next step should be to strengthen the connective tissue between them.

A Criminal Justice Advisory Commission would provide one possible institutional mechanism for doing precisely that, helping Malaysia move from reactive criminal justice policymaking towards a more coordinated, evidence-based and forward-looking system of justice, public safety and rehabilitation.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia and an FMT reader.

3442c9fdac4b6ecf: Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir’s recent dismissal of the entire executive council has left Negeri Sembilan in limbo.
Menteri besar Ismail Lasim has been left to run the administration alone, relying on civil servants to keep the machinery of government moving.
At the Aug 1 state election, Barisan Nasional won 18 of the 36 state assembly seats on offer, one short of an outright simple majority—and was only propped up by support from PAS.

Initially, Jalaluddin Alias—the man who led Umno’s withdrawal of support for the previous administration—was tipped to take over as MB. However, it was Ismail who was sworn in, with Jalaluddin overlooked even for a seat on the 10-man exco lineup.
Ismail himself has been mired in controversy.

Soon after pledging his allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz, he signed a proclamation seeking the ruler’s removal, then disavowed it on grounds of coercion, before affirming it again—this time unanimously with the rest of his exco.
That last act was enough for the entire exco to be sacked on grounds of disloyalty to the ruler, leaving Ismail the last man standing.
Ismail may have survived the cull, but was his own conduct proper? Does he still have the moral authority to remain menteri besar?
Even if he clings to office, Ismail cannot form a functioning exco. His entire 10-man team has already betrayed the ruler and been sacked. Surely, they cannot be reappointed.
With Jalaluddin presumably not in contention, Ismail is left to choose from the assemblymen he originally bypassed. But do Negeri Sembilan voters deserve a government of second-choice leaders?
Previous legitimacy crises
Malaysia has faced constitutional turmoil before.

In 1977, Kelantan plunged into crisis when PAS clashed with Umno, prompting an emergency and suspension of the state assembly. In 2009, Perak’s defections sparked a bitter legal battle over who commanded the confidence of the house.
In both cases, governance collapsed when legitimacy was in doubt.

So what of Negeri Sembilan today? Who will debate land policies, laws, and budgets? Who will table motions, approve bills, and scrutinize expenditure? Who will raise constituency issues on behalf of voters?
Time to face the truth
The reality is stark. BN, despite its numbers, has no clear path to government and stability. In any case, Negeri Sembilan’s people deserve better.
The time for political games is over.
Either dissolve the assembly and return the mandate to the people, or accept that only a unity government can salvage what remains of Negeri Sembilan’s dignity.
Anything less would be a betrayal of the state and its citizens.
The writer is a senior journalist at FMT’s English Desk.

e63a673e0be8bc0f: "Rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea," Lukas Vogel writes in a lengthy blog post explaining how exactly he managed to render Doom using an SQL database.

OK, that's not entirely accurate. The SQLDoom project uses a small Python client to handle input and output, drive the game's timing, and display each frame to the screen. Behind that, a series of CedarDB tables tracks the game geometry and state, while about 1,300 lines of SQL queries spread across 89 common table expressions implement the game logic and generate 35 bitmap framebuffers per second.

In this, SQLDoom is a major improvement over Vogel's previous DoomQL project, which last year set out to build "a multiplayer Doom-like shooter entirely in SQL." Unfortunately, that effort ended up with raycasting-based, grayscale ASCII graphics that were more akin to the simplistic 90-degree-angled maps of Wolfenstein 3D. The newer SQLDoom, on the other hand, generates full-color 640x480 frames that look like they could have come from the original Doom executable.
