5a3d5ff447508845: The grief that swept across Malaysia following the passing of Dr Hasmah Ali, wife of former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad, was nothing short of extraordinary.
It was a heartfelt farewell befitting the nation’s most beloved First Lady — a woman whose unwavering presence beside her husband was a story of devotion in itself.

And the tributes have not stopped. From Malaysians of every race, every creed, every walk of life, the outpouring has been relentless — a rare sight that has moved many to tears. Even days after her final bow, the love remains.
But it was a scene in Hasmah’s final send-off that will forever be etched in the hearts of Malaysians yearning for unity. A scene that spoke louder than any policy or speech.
There was Mahathir, at 101 years old, in his wheelchair, tears streaming down his face as he bade farewell to his partner of a lifetime.

And standing behind him, in a silent show of solidarity, were three individuals: a Malay doctor, an Indian nurse, and a Chinese physiotherapist. The physiotherapist, himself fighting back tears, gently held tissues to wipe away the former PM’s tears, ensuring he was okay.
It was a fleeting moment, but it said everything.

This was the dream. This was the “Bangsa Malaysia” that Mahathir envisioned when he launched Vision 2020 back in 1991. Sadly, it never fully materialised even though he returned for a second stint in office in 2018.
But here, inadvertently and coincidentally, at the most vulnerable moment of his life, the nation watched it unfold “live”.
It was a powerful reminder that Malaysia cannot survive, cannot thrive, without all its citizens — each playing their part, especially when times are tough.

This was how the older generations lived. This was how they built the nation. Race and religion were afterthoughts; what mattered was the Malaysian standing before them, bringing glory to the nation, regardless of skin colour.
And then there were the pictures.

Two photographs posted by badminton legend Lee Chong Wei in his tear-jerking tribute to Hasmah — whom he lovingly called a motherly figure to him and his wife. As patron of the Badminton Association of Malaysia during Chong Wei’s glorious reign, she was more than a figurehead; she was family.

In the first photo, Chong Wei is seen walking forward, hand outstretched in greeting. But what happened next took everyone’s breath away. Hasmah, instead of a formal handshake, opened her arms wide and pulled him into a warm, enveloping hug.
It was a simple gesture. But in that embrace, she showed Malaysians something profound: that despite our different colours and creeds, we are, and always will be, one race. The human race.
There is so much for Malaysian politicians to learn from this episode.
There were more instances that showed the Malaysian in Hasmah but you need to write a book to document everything.
Rest in peace, Hasmah. You taught us how to live, how to love, and in your passing, how to unite.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
11b9d330370e3dd5: There was something slightly strange about watching Malaysian athletics in Nagoya.
Some of the loudest Malaysian cheers belonged to two sprinters wearing Thai and Singaporean colours.
Puripol Boonson came tearing down the home straight and it was impossible not to watch. Shanti Pereira emerged from the bend in the rain and Malaysians could only marvel.
Perhaps that is what sport is supposed to do. Excellence has no passport.
But it also leaves Malaysian athletics with an uncomfortable question.
What happens when a country’s supporters begin looking across the border for something to believe in?
Boonson gave them plenty.

The 20-year-old Thai won the 100m in 9.90 seconds, a Games record, then produced an astonishing 19.88 in the 200m to complete the sprint double. His 200m time matched China’s Xie Zhenye’s Asian record.
His race had a particular drama. The start was not spectacular. Then he began to eat up the bend before powering into the straight, opening daylight between himself and the field.
Pereira provided a different kind of spectacle.

On a rain-swept track, the Singaporean defended her 200m title in 22.78 seconds. She did not have the fastest start, but built her race around the curve before producing the strongest finish. She became the first woman to win the Asian Games 200m twice.
These were not simply victories. They looked like performances built on purpose.
That is where the comparison with Malaysia becomes uncomfortable.
Malaysia sent 20 athletes to the athletics programme. Only Azeem Fahmi and Danish Iftikhar Roslee reached individual finals, in the 100m and 200m respectively.
Azeem's race ended painfully when muscle cramps forced him to slow almost to a walk before he crossed in 14.65 seconds. Danish finished sixth in 20.89.
There were young athletes who gained experience and made progress. That should be acknowledged. But too many performances offered little evidence of where the next breakthrough might come from.
And this was not an isolated bad week.
The last two years have brought coaching disputes, questions over athlete development and competition, organisational controversies and a growing sense of drift.
There have been changes and new structures, but Nagoya should force a more prickly question: have those changes actually improved the system?
There are no quick fixes for an illness. But before treatment can begin, someone has to admit the patient is sick.
The worrying thing about Malaysian athletics is not simply that it has come home without a medal. It is whether there is enough urgency to suggest that the result has forced a reckoning.
If Malaysia Athletics thinks Nagoya was an aberration, it risks adding another problem to the list: self-delusion.

Athletics is brutally competitive. Malaysia is not simply competing against its Southeast Asian neighbours. Seventeen countries had won athletics medals in Nagoya, while Malaysia remained outside the medal table.
That should temper the argument, not weaken it.
The question is not why Malaysia did not beat China, Japan or India.
It is why neighbouring countries are producing athletes capable of making Asia sit up and watch.
Look at Boonson.
His development stretches back through school athletics and national structures, with coaching support that has continued to evolve as he has moved towards the senior level.
Look at Pereira.

Her progress has been built over years with coach Luis Cunha, who has worked on the smallest details of her sprinting, from mechanics to acceleration and the ability to squeeze more from an already accomplished athlete.
That is the comparison worth making.
Not whether Thailand or Singapore has discovered a secret formula. But whether Malaysia has built an environment in which talented athletes can keep getting better.
Danish, 19, offers a revealing case.

At last year’s SEA Games, he finished third in the 100m and 200m behind Boonson. He has since emerged as one of Malaysia's most promising young sprinters, holding the national 200m record of 20.73 seconds.
That is progress, but Boonson was progressing too. What is Thailand doing to keep moving its young sprinter forward? That is a system question, not an indictment of Danish.
The same distinction must apply across the Malaysian team. Athletes are responsible for their training, discipline, recovery and performance.

They cannot build the national development system around them, recruit specialist coaches, create an international competition programme, resolve disputes between associations or determine how promising juniors are identified and moved into the senior ranks.
This is where Malaysia Athletics needs to be honest. Where is the pathway from junior to senior athletics? How many athletes who emerge at Sukma become international contenders?

How are coaches evaluated and what happens when an athlete stagnates? What level of sports-science support is available, and how much meaningful international competition do promising athletes receive?
Most importantly, who is accountable when the system does not deliver?
There are encouraging signs. Nine Sukma records were broken at the 2026 Games, suggesting Malaysia still has young athletes capable of progress.
But what happens to that progression once they move from promising youngster to senior international athlete?

Malaysia Athletics should consider an independent examination of its high-performance system covering coaching, talent identification, junior development, state associations, competition planning, sports science, athlete welfare, selection and funding.
This should not become a hunt for convenient scapegoats. It should begin with a more basic question: what did Malaysia Athletics promise, and what did it actually deliver?
The answer matters because Kuala Lumpur hosts the SEA Games next year.
Home advantage can produce medals. It cannot manufacture a high-performance system.
A successful SEA Games could even make the problem harder to see. Malaysia might win medals on home soil and declare that the worst is over.
But the real test will be whether the athletes who emerge in Kuala Lumpur have a pathway beyond the Games.
That is what Boonson and Pereira represent — continuity.

Pereira's success has been built around an athlete and coach who have worked together for years. Boonson's performances show what can happen when youthful talent continues to move forward instead of merely being celebrated for its potential. Malaysia needs that progression.
Perhaps that explains why Malaysians found themselves cheering for Boonson and Pereira.
Fans do not owe a flag their admiration. They give it to excellence when they see it.
Boonson made the track feel fast. Pereira made it feel dramatic. They gave spectators something to believe in.
Malaysian athletics needs to give Malaysians that feeling again.
Not through slogans. Not through another restructuring exercise. Not by promising that the next Games will be different.
But by building athletes who can walk onto an Asian track and look as though they belong there.
There is less than a year before the SEA Games come to Kuala Lumpur.
That is not enough time to repair everything. It is enough time to decide whether Nagoya was a warning or merely another result.
The first step is not winning a medal — it is admitting there is a problem.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
5b1fa80e5759bf96: Sultan Perak, Sultan Nazrin Shah secara agak mendadak dan tiba-tiba menzahirkan dukacita mendalam baginda terhadap budaya perbincangan dan perdebatan, yang menurutnya sudah menjauhi muafakat, tetapi mengarah kepada pertelagahan tanpa adab. Sudah tentu, Sultan Nazrin bertitah dan menegur gejala cita bencana ini dalam kalangan masyarakat Melayu dan umat Islam di negara ini.

Sultan Nazrin dilaporkan membuka titah tersebut ketika mempengerusikan mesyuarat Majlis Kebangsaan Bagi Hal Ehwal Agama Islam (MKI) yang mana baginda adalah pengerusinya. Sultan Nazrin seterusnya dikatakan khuatir dengan gejala berita yang belum disahkan, tetapi disebarkan, penelanjangan aib selain perbezaan pandangan yang sepatutnya kecil kini bertukar menjadi permusuhan.

Titah Baginda: "Sangat mendukacitakan, malah bertambah mengaibkan, ketika ini kita menyaksikan perbincangan dan perdebatan, yang lebih berbentuk pertelagahan tanpa adab, sedang dan semakin berlaku dalam kalangan masyarakat Melayu dan umat Islam di negara ini. Berita yang belum disahihkan, disebarkan tanpa menghiraukan dosa, aib dibuka dan perbezaan pandangan bertukar menjadi permusuhan. Amatlah penting bagi bangsa kita dan umat Islam, dididik membudayakan sikap mendengar sebelum menjawab, memahami sebelum menghukum dan meneliti sebelum menyebarkan sesuatu.”

Kebimbangan Sultan Nazrin itu ternyata mendalam kerana Baginda turut mengingatkan masyarakat supaya 'tidak menjadi insan yang hanya mahu didengar tetapi tidak mahu mendengar, mudah menghukum tetapi enggan memahami atau berbicara mengenai perpaduan sedangkan kata-kata sendiri menyalakan perpecahan'.

Sebenarnya, fenomena cita bencana yang disebut-sebut oleh Sultan Nazrin itu boleh dikesani paling banyak tumbuh melalang di pelbagai platform media sosial. Masing-masing mengulas, mengomentar, menulis pandangan tanpa tapis, tanpa berfikir dan tidak mengingat dosa.

Dalam krisis yang menimpa Negeri Sembilan, kini telah berlarutan hampir enam bulan; fitnah mengenai tanah adat, waris-waris bertikai, dan aneka macam lagi, tampak menjadi-jadi. Media menggunakan istilah kemelut untuk menggambarkan konflik gila ini. Tetapi, sebenarnya tiada kemelut. Yang ada hanyalah 'ke-mulut'. Atau, kemulut.

Mengapakah ia bukan kemelut? Tetapi kemulut? Apakah kemelut dan apakah kemulut? Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka menghurai kemelut sebagai keadaan atau saat genting lagi berbahaya dan ia adalah berkenaan ekonomi, atau politik, di mana ia ditanggapi semacam satu kegen­tingan, krisis, atau dalam erti kata lain kebalikan kepada kestabilan dan keharmonian.

Kemulut adalah satu istilah ciptaan sendiri untuk memaparkan secara palsu satu-satu keadaan atau saat itu sebagai genting lagi berbahaya demi agenda atau objektif politik tertentu yang biasanya adalah untuk beroleh kuasa, keuntungan bisnes, projek, atau melepaskan diri dari satu-satu hukuman jenayah seperti contohnya rasuah, dan korupsi. Kemulut dinamai kemulut kerana mereka yang bekerja untuk memalsukan keadaan ini akan beroleh upah berbayar, wang habuan, gaji hadiah supaya kegentingan berterusan sehinggalah kelak padam sendiri lantaran basi atau dalam bahasa Inggeris, overtaken by events.

Gejala kemulut ini sangat berkait rapat dengan gerakan politik lasykar siber satu terma atau istilah digunakan untuk menjelaskan perihal aktivis parti politik yang diupah untuk membenih, menyebar dan menggandakan kesan propaganda politik di media. Kepesatan media sosial menjadikan mereka ini dikesani dengan mudah di Facebook, TikTok atau X. Fenomena kemulut lasykar siber ini mula dikesani dengan ketara ketika kempen PRU-12 dan meledak menjelang pilihan raya ke-14, dan ke-15. Ia semakin menjadi-jadi sekarang memandangkan suhu politik di negara kita kian menaik ekoran siri pilihan raya di Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka tidak lama lagi.

Gerakan lasykar siber tidak sama dengan kekecohan para warganet atau jaguh siber. Kedua-dua gelar ini, warganet dan juara siber biasanya adalah organik dan merupakan reaksi spontan tanpa terstruktur. Namun, keberadaan warganet dan jaguh siber ini sangat rapat dengan lasykar siber. Sebagai satu bandingan, lasykar siber menanam benih atau naratif politik tertentu, dan mereka itu berbayar, dan apabila sesuatu isu menjadi genting dan kemelut, warganet dan jaguh siber yang terdiri dari pengguna media sosial orang awam akan memberi reaksi segera atau spontan. Warganet dan jaguh siber ini tidak dibayar, dan kadangkala memberi respons biadab, antiadab, menyala-nyalakan pergaduhan dan seperti digambarkan oleh baginda Sultan Perak sebagai degil dan hanya mahu didengar tetapi enggan mendengar, cepat melompat menghukum seraya sengaja menolak untuk memahami sesuatu isu itu. Kebiasaannya tukang bakar iaitu lasykar siber ini akan terus mengapi-apikan keadaan dengan menjadikan nafsu ketaasuban sebagai kayu bakar.
Warganet dan jaguh siber yang tidak tahu dalang di sebalik kemulut itu akan terus menari mengikut rentak mereka.

Fenomena kemulut ini dalam ilmu sains politik adalah apa yang dinamakan sebagai political astroturfing. Para kemulut ini tahu bila perlu bertindak, dan mempunyai mekanisme tindak balas yang teratur untuk mengurang atau menggandakan impak kegiatan mereka. Rauchfleisch Kovic, dalam penerbitan ilmiah bertajuk 'Digital astroturfing in politics: Definition, typology and countermeasures' pada 2018 dan terbit di jurnal bernama Studies in Communication Sciences, menyatakan political astroturfing ini ialah satu kaedah atau gerakan, kempen atau aktiviti politik dalam talian yang ditonjolkan sebagai sekadar aktiviti individu biasa atau orang awam, tetapi sebenarnya mereka adalah aktor politik berbayar (justeru kemulut) dan terdapat tuan atau majikan politik yang menggunakan khidmat mereka untuk terus-terusan menggerakkan aktiviti sebegini.

Political astroturfing, bukan gerakan atau sentimen akar umbi yang tulen tetapi ia ditampil sedemikian. Dalam banyak keadaan ia adalah kegiatan terancang dan diatur secara terpusat dari atas ke bawah. Political astroturfing juga adalah siri kempen maklumat palsu yang telah diprogramkan secara berpusat menerusi penyamaran identiti. Ia berlaku dengan pesat dalam talian dengan agenda mewujudkan satu bentuk penyelewengan maklumat bertujuan untuk mencipta tanggapan palsu bahawa sikap atau pandangan yang dilontar mereka itu mendapat sokongan meluas dalam masyarakat.

Kesimpulannya, political astroturfing adalah taktik aktor politik untuk mengelirukan masyarakat dengan informasi palsu, dengan menggunakan identiti atau profil palsu dengan maksud untuk memperdayakan masyarakat.

Astroturfing ini sudah tentu tidak mementingkan adab. Ia mementingkan mulut, dan perut; wang atau habuan, upah atau janji majikannya; di mana selalu bos mereka adalah parti atau tokoh politik. Justeru astroturfing ini berkait rapat dengan lasykar siber, yang bekerja mencipta kemelut untuk beroleh sesuatu ke mulut mereka. Warganet dan jaguh siber pula adalah mereka yang ditenggek.

Astroturfing, bukanlah political bots yang mana ia merujuk secara ringkasnya perkongsian konten media sosial dengan masyarakat secara khusus mengenai isu politik. Political bots ini tidak semestinya berniat jahat dan berkongsi maklumat palsu. Terdapat dalam kalangan mereka memang menumpukan masa terluang untuk berkongsi maklumat politik yang sahih, benar dan relevan, dan selalunya mereka tiada kesetiaan kepada sesuatu isu atau bos tertentu. Mereka secara jujur menggunakan medium media sosial sebagai suara politik mereka. Kejujuran mereka dapat dikenal pasti memandangkan kelompok ini tidak menggunakan akaun palsu, sebaliknya mempunyai akaun atau profil yang sah.

Ada kemungkinan besar kemelut di Negeri Sembilan misalnya digerakkan oleh kemulut sesetengah pihak yang berkepentingan. Mungkin, kemulut yang bertanggungjawab menciptakan kemelut di Negeri Sembilan itu beroleh kelulut lazat. Mungkin, tumpuan awal mereka adalah untuk mencipta ketidakstabilan politik di negeri tersebut dengan maksud untuk berlaku pilihan raya awal. Tujuan pilihan raya awal ini katakan, adalah untuk membolot kekayaan dan hasil mahsul negeri khusus dalam bentuk nadir bumi. Mudah-mudah orang awam, atau warganet biasa yang jahil pun terpedaya dan tertipu oleh kemulut ini.

Kemulut terus-terusan membakar dan memanjangkan kemelut yang kadang turun, dan tiba-tiba mencanak naik. Seperti yang telah dijelaskan dalam kerangka political astroturfing, untuk memadamkan kemelut ini, kita mestilah menyergap kemulut dan melacak siapa dalang di belakang mereka. Kemulut, sesuai dengan istilahnya selalu dibayar lumayan. Tidak susah mana pun untuk memastikan punca wang mereka itu. Jika dijejak kita tahu jembalangnya.
Apabila kemulut ini dikenal pasti, dan dipatahkan gerakan mereka, negeri atau negara akan aman semula. Dan Insya-Allah, seperti diharapkan oleh baginda Sultan Nazrin itu, adab akan kembali.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
1999d70e31b9acfb: Malaysia’s foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has raised one of the oldest and most uncomfortable questions surrounding the United Nations: why should five countries possess the power to prevent the UN Security Council from acting?
His argument that the veto should be challenged and ultimately abolished deserves serious attention. Expanding the Security Council alone cannot resolve its structural weaknesses.

More countries sitting around the table will mean little if five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — continue to hold powers unavailable to everyone else.
Yet there is an enormous difference between recognising the problem and solving it.
Abolishing the veto is practical as an aspiration but almost impossible under the present international system.
The reason is straightforward.
The veto was not accidentally inserted into the UN Charter.
It was part of the political bargain underpinning the creation of the United Nations after the Second World War.
The major powers would participate in the new organisation so long as they could prevent decisions on substantive Security Council matters that fundamentally contradicted their interests.
That arrangement remains deeply entrenched.
Indeed, changing the UN Charter requires ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent Security Council members.
The paradox could hardly be clearer: the countries that possess the veto effectively possess a veto over abolishing their own veto.
Why would they voluntarily surrender it?
Washington regards permanent membership and the veto as important instruments of American influence. Beijing and Moscow view theirs similarly.
London and Paris are unlikely to surrender one of the principal institutional privileges maintaining their status as permanent Security Council powers.
Great powers rarely relinquish entrenched advantages merely because others regard them as unfair.
Nevertheless, Mohamad is correct to challenge the principle.
The world of 2026 bears little resemblance to that of 1945.
India is among the world’s most important powers. Africa, despite having more than 50 UN members, lacks permanent representation.
Neither Latin America nor Southeast Asia possesses a permanent seat.
The Security Council therefore continues to carry the institutional DNA of the immediate postwar order.
Expanding its membership would improve representation.
But expansion without addressing the veto could merely create a larger council while preserving its fundamental inequality.
This is where Malaysia and other middle powers should concentrate their diplomatic efforts.
If immediate abolition is virtually impossible, constraining the political use of the veto is not.
The UN General Assembly has already established a mechanism requiring scrutiny when a permanent Security Council member exercises its veto.
Such mechanisms should be strengthened, particularly when the council is considering genocide, crimes against humanity or other grave violations of international humanitarian law.
Every veto should carry a political cost.
The permanent member using it should have to explain publicly why preventing collective action serves international peace and security.
The General Assembly should become increasingly assertive whenever the Security Council becomes paralysed.
For Asean, there is an important lesson here.
Southeast Asian countries cannot compete militarily with the major powers.
Asean’s influence has instead depended on consultation, institutional persistence, consensus and moral suasion.
Small and middle powers survive in an unequal international system not by pretending that power does not exist, but by creating rules and expectations that constrain how power is exercised.
The same principle should apply to the United Nations.
There is also a warning for the permanent five themselves.
The veto protects their national interests, but excessive reliance on it can progressively weaken the institution from which their privileged status derives.
If the Security Council repeatedly becomes incapable of acting precisely when international peace is most endangered, countries will increasingly seek other coalitions, institutions and arrangements.
The veto can therefore protect power while simultaneously eroding legitimacy.
Malaysia should consequently continue challenging it, even while recognising that formal abolition remains extraordinarily difficult.
International norms rarely disappear overnight. They weaken when practices once considered unquestionable become progressively harder to justify.
The veto emerged from the geopolitical realities of 1945. Eight decades later, the international community has every right to question whether those privileges should remain permanent.
Removing them presently may be close to impossible.
But allowing entrenched privilege to remain permanently beyond challenge would be worse.
It would leave the United Nations not merely constrained by great-power politics but increasingly imprisoned by it.
Asean has to keep expressing its opposition to a permanent system of great power privilege without end though.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
fd382010ba317855: In 1947, a young Malay woman entered medical school in Singapore; she was the only Malay woman in her intake. I wonder what it felt like to walk into that classroom each morning, knowing there was nobody quite like you there.

Dr Hasmah Ali, also known as Siti Hasmah, went on to graduate, practise medicine and lead public health services. With her passing at the age of 100, we have lost someone who helped change what a doctor could look like in Malaysia.

Many knew her as the wife of a prime minister. She was that, and carried the role for decades, but she was a doctor before she was a public figure, and her medical work deserves to be remembered on its own terms.

After graduating in 1955, she worked in a hospital before devoting herself to maternal and child health in Kedah. In 1965, she became the first woman to be appointed as a medical officer in the maternal and child health department; in 1974, she became the state’s first female maternal and child health officer. She also led the rural health training school in Jitra.
Those appointments gave her responsibility for people’s care and for the health workers who would provide it.
Her teams travelled to villages to provide immunisation and health education. They worked with traditional midwives and spoke with families about pregnancy, childbirth and caring for newborns.

Hasmah understood that a mother could not always arrange transport, leave her responsibilities and appear at a clinic simply because a doctor wanted her there. Healthcare had to make the journey towards her.

I find that part of her story especially moving. It is easy to praise a pioneer for being a trailblazer. It takes longer to understand the patient work that followed: returning to communities, earning trust and teaching others to care for mothers and children.
She helped build a health service in which a woman’s judgment could guide that work.

The norm she challenged has changed profoundly for Malaysian women who came after her such as Dr Narimah Awin, who went on to lead family health services and advise the World Health Organization on maternal and reproductive health; Dr Adeeba Kamarulzaman, whose work on HIV took her into global leadership; and Dr Jemilah Mahmood, who founded Mercy Malaysia and now leads work in planetary health.

And of course, Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, who took her experience as a doctor into national political life while continuing to support programmes and changes within the health landscape. Most recently, Dr BP Nirmala, a Malaysian cancer epidemiologist, joined the World Health Organization (WHO) science council this year.

For me, this is also personal. Dr S Saunthari leads the National Cancer Society of Malaysia, of which I now serve as a director. She is also the first Malaysian president-elect of the global NCD Alliance.

Around these well-known names are many more women leading wards, district services, classrooms and research teams. Each has earned their place. Together, they show how far women’s authority in medicine now reaches.
Hasmah lived another side of medicine when she was treated for breast cancer. In 2019, she spoke publicly about that experience.

The doctor who had spent years urging women to care for their health let us hear from her as a patient. Her illness did not define her life, but her willingness to speak about it was another way of making women’s health visible.

We should be careful not to assume that there is a straight line from one woman to the next. Hasmah did not create every opportunity that followed, and the women who came after her built their own careers.

But the legacy of her achievement was to help change expectations of them. She showed Malaysians a Malay woman practising medicine, teaching health workers and leading a service at a time when that was a rare sight.

She remains an icon because her example still asks something of us. When a young woman finds herself the only one in the room, will we recognise her ability and make room for her to lead? When a patient cannot reach care, will we go closer to them?
Hasmah answered those questions with her life. Her light continues in the women who enter medicine, in those who lead it, and in the people whose lives they change.

And as much as we will remember the former prime minister’s wife, we will also remember the doctor who went to mothers in the villages of Kedah, the teacher who prepared others to care for them, and the woman who spoke openly when she herself faced cancer.
Hasmah was always her own woman. Her work lives on in the people it reached; her example lives on in the women who follow. And she will remain, very dearly, in our hearts.

The Transit Lab’s winning project, the Public Transit Intelligence Hub (PTIQ), aims to unify public transportation agencies’ real-time monitoring, operations control, and passenger communication systems into a single centralized AI-orchestrated platform that will allow transit control center staff to make better-informed, on-the-spot decisions, and provide riders with more immediate and accurate information. The PTIQ program manager is MIT Lecturer Jim Aloisi, who directs the Transit Research Consortium, which will also work on the project. That consortium is comprised of researchers from the Transit Lab, MMI, and Northeastern University, where Professor Haris Koutsopoulos takes the lead.  In addition to providing funding for the three-year project, Google.org will provide pro bono support from its own engineers and AI product experts. "AI holds incredible potential to transform public services, but there is often a gap between promise and practice,” says Maggie Johnson, global head of Google.org. “By equipping the 15 selected organizations with funding and pro bono support from Google's own AI experts, we are empowering the people closest to the problem to show what is truly possible. Public transit is assessed in the control center and on the streets. Over decades of work with transit agencies in Washington, D.C., Chicago, London, Boston, Tokyo, and Hong Kong, we have learned to ask a different question. PTIQ is designed to ground AI in the institutional reality and behavioral nuances of a transit agency, and bring machine intelligence and human judgment into one place.” “Currently the evaluation of AI models relies heavily on deterministic, objective tasks, such as solving mathematical equations or generating code,” Abdelhalim explains. “However, the vast majority of real-world operational tasks — like delivering public transit services — are highly dynamic, multi-stakeholder, and lack a single correct objective answer. ea039df066f8591e: A new AI system that excels at challenging games with hidden information could someday help human decision-makers select ideal strategies to outfox opponents in complicated situations like military maneuvers. Using advances in machine-learning, researchers from MIT, Carnegie Mellon University, New York University, and Stanford University developed an AI that defeated top-ranked human players of the board wargame Stratego by a large margin — something no AI system had been able to achieve.  Stratego, a two-player game of imperfect information, in which the opponent’s piece identities remain hidden, is often used as a benchmark to test the strategic thinking abilities of powerful AI models. To build their model, the researchers combined efficient training algorithms with new techniques tailored for calculated decision-making in hidden information settings.  The AI system achieved greater performance at Stratego than the next best models, while being far cheaper and less computationally demanding to train. The system also outperformed top human players in other strategic games with different rules and designs, demonstrating how it can be generalized for a variety of use-cases. The AI system could be adapted to help humans tackle many real-world problems with hidden information, such as business negotiations or cybersecurity.  “In the kind of imperfect information tasks you would face in reality, you often don’t have the luxury of enumerating through all the possibilities. There are just too many. Having AI algorithms that are general purpose and can provably perform this challenging task so well is a big step forward,” says Gabriele Farina, an assistant professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), principal investigator at the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), and senior author of a paper on this AI system. He is joined on the paper by lead author Samuel Sokota, a graduate student at Carnegie Mellon; Eugene Vinitsky, an assistant professor at NYU; Zico Kolter, a professor at Carnegie Mellon; Hengyuan Hu, a graduate student at Stanford; and Zhiyuan Fan, an EECS graduate student at MIT. The research appears today in Nature. Hidden information The world is full of imperfect information problems.  In these interactions, some parties possess information others do not. For instance, traders in financial markets may not know the rationale behind the trades of others, while military forces likely don’t have full knowledge of enemy positions.  With hidden information, the decisions parties make, as well as the decisions they choose not to make, are intertwined in such a way that it is extremely difficult to determine the best steps to take next. “The more you bluff, the more your opponent expects it, and the less each bluff is worth. It’s not obvious how to reason about that,” Sokota explains. “It’s very different from a setting like chess, where the best move is still the best move no matter how often you’ve played it.” Stratego is often used to model imperfect information situations. In this board wargame, which resembles military chess, players arrange 40 pieces on their side of a board and then move pieces across the board to capture their opponent’s flag.  But the identity of all pieces remains secret until they collide, and then the lower-ranking piece is eliminated. The possible piece configurations number more than 10 to the 66th power — an exponentially greater number than in chess — making Stratego extremely difficult for an AI system to play well.  Past efforts, such as Google’s DeepMind, relied on sophisticated operations that were computationally demanding and costly. But even with millions of dollars in training costs, these models were still not strong enough to beat top human Stratego players. “With Stratego, there is an explosion of possible universes you might have to deal with. AI techniques that were developed for games like poker definitely could not scale in this setting,” Farina says. The MIT researchers set out to develop a full AI system that could achieve superhuman performance for less cost, which they called Ataraxos (a Greek word used to describe one who is unbothered or free from anxiety). A two-pronged approach To build Ataraxos, the researchers trained the model using a technique called self-play reinforcement learning. The model plays against itself many times to learn a strong “blueprint strategy” of how to excel at Stratego.  They designed especially efficient algorithms, which enabled Ataraxos to learn much faster than prior methods while ensuring it didn’t get stuck trying to predict every possible move. This reduces training costs and boosts performance.  “Our system reaches strictly higher playing strength than DeepNash (DeepMind’s system) while using less than one hundredth of the training examples and less than one thirtieth of the self-play games, indicating a massive improvement in efficiency,” says Farina. During a game, Ataraxos uses the blueprint strategy as a starting point to set up the board and begin thinking about its next moves at each round of play.  But before acting, it refines its choices on the fly using a technique called decision-time planning. The system employs a generative model that uses probabilities to estimate the likely identities of the opponent’s hidden pieces, then evaluates future choices before selecting the next move.  “Rather than just guessing blindly, we use decision-time planning to find the most plausible state of the board. Using this generative model allows us to really zoom in on the specific board and opponent we are facing,” Farina says. The innovative use of this generative model for decision-time planning was the missing piece that enabled Ataraxos to achieve superhuman performance. Ataraxos beat the strongest Stratego player in the world by a record margin of 15-1-4 and achieved a 39-2 record against top human players at the Stratego world championship. “Ataraxos is good at calculating risk in a way that humans are not. A human might start freaking out if their most valuable piece is exposed, but the bot can be surprisingly composed. It doesn’t overcorrect and give away its secrets,” Farina says. The researchers also adapted Ataraxos for other imperfect information games, including Barrage Stratego (a faster-paced variant with fewer pieces), Hanabi (a cooperative card game with many players), and Dou dizhu (a game in which two players cooperate against a third). The system achieved superhuman performance in each instance, demonstrating the generality of this method. In the future, the researchers want to build interpretability measures into Ataraxos so the system can explain its decision-making in a way that a human could understand.  “Humans must have the final say in whether a recommendation is followed, so before adoption can happen, we need a way to audit the model’s decisions. We still have a long way to go, but I hope these algorithms can be the foundation for a lot more work to come,” Farina says. This research is funded, in part, by the Office of Naval Research, the New York University Department of Civil and Urban Engineering, the C2SMART Center, the National Science Foundation, and a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Early Career Fellowship.

9e7b8b5e56b75166: Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face, OpenAI is still putting out fires. A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology.

Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system. The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened.

But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer.
Chen oversees OpenAI’s research teams. The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch. In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.
I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem.

Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident—the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to.

Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models. A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place. We are working on these now. This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks.

The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry. And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says.
Out of control
Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part.

“When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.”
The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix.

But Chen insists that OpenAI is on it. He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack. In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.

“It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.”

At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards. In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working.
What’s changed
I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control.

“Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there. There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure. We’ve taken it very seriously. We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.”

The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says.

OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models. It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought—the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results. In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human.
Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed. Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well.

“We didn’t have the monitors on in training before. It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.”
Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring.
OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says.

All of which sounds sensible. But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming?

“Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.”

The signs were there, but they were misread. Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts, a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen.

According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives, including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.

An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster. We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar. We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”
Race vs. pace

OpenAI’s rivals have taken note. Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down. But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs?

“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm. The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.”

Coordination across US companies will be hard enough. Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security. If a global race continues, what then? And what about open-source models from outfits beyond the reach of US regulations?

Chen dropped his upbeat manner for the first time in our conversation: “I do think we have to prepare for a world where, say, six months to a year out, we have open-source models with the capability of the agents behind the Hugging Face incident, but which are deliberately misaligned to go attack infrastructure or create harm in the world.”

What that world needs most, says Chen, is OpenAI. “If you entertain for a moment that OpenAI is one of the companies that cares most about alignment—and I believe this to be true; it can be debated, but I really do think it’s true—then if you disappear OpenAI, that would be bad for the world.”
Existential risks
What about the more extreme claims made by some of his Silicon Valley peers that AI could kill us all—and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are not doing enough to stop it?
“Researchers are a heterogeneous group of people, you know, with beliefs across the spectrum,” he says.

“Personally, I don’t think we have to be resigned to there being some probability that we’re all going to be existentially at risk. We have agency over this. We are not going to go and deploy models if they truly have that kind of probability of causing a risk to humanity. At a frontier lab, you have the ability to work on alignment to the point that you do not feel like you’re incurring more than epsilon risk to the world in deploying your models.”
(In discussions about levels of risk, the Greek letter epsilon is often used as a mathematical placeholder for an acceptable threshold. Chen doesn’t say what his epsilon would be.)

When tech leaders are asked to justify the downsides of AI, their go-to talking point is that the upsides—from helping cure diseases to coming up with cleaner sources of energy—far outweigh the immediate costs. Short-term pains, long-term gains.

But as the downsides pile up, does that case get harder to make? Is there a point where Chen would feel less as if he’s building something amazing and more as if he’s simply minimizing harm—fighting fires rather than forging a better future?

The capabilities of these models are already evident, he says: “It is time to start delivering the benefits of AI to humanity. It’s time to start working on deep problems in drug discovery, on materials, on scientific applications that will actually change people’s lives.”

“Yes, there is a bit of risk that we are incurring, but we see all these benefits,” he adds. “I think we should make that less of an abstract thing. If people can really see the upside, I think they’ll believe in it.”

ee237f4f3037e6a8: From Moaz Nair

Death serves as a unifier rather than a divider. It is profoundly regrettable when a preacher, whose primary responsibility is to convey a message of peace, chooses to harbour bad assumptions regarding the presence of political leaders at the final respects for the late Dr Hasmah Ali.

Labelling the courtesy visit as an act of "hypocrisy" or "merely trying to look good" not only disregards the obligations of fard kifayah (communal obligation) but also violates the moral guidelines outlined in Surah Al-Hujurat, verse 11, which admonishes against belittling the deeds of others.
Politics has its boundaries, and those boundaries dissolve when the inevitability of death arrives.
In this heightened domestic political climate, the line separating ideological differences from jurisprudential obligations (shariah) at times appears to be increasingly blurred.

As preachers entrusted with conveying religious messages, a fundamental question must be collectively examined: is it appropriate for an agent of dakwah (religious propagation) to vilify opponents and question the act of paying respects to the deceased on grounds of political differences?
Examining the true framework of Islamic propagation reveals a clear answer. Vilifying opponents – whether within political or personal spheres – is strictly prohibited.
Conversely, paying respects to the deceased, regardless of whether they were ideological allies or political adversaries, represents a highly commendable virtue and moral imperative.
The voice of dakwah: healing, not destroying
The ruling against vilifying political adversaries in Islam contains no grey areas; it is forbidden (haram) and should never escape the lips of a Muslim, let alone a preacher.

The primary duty of a practitioner of dakwah (da’i) is to invite humanity towards goodness through wisdom and excellent counsel (al-mau'izah al-hasanah), rather than spewing insults on stages or social media platforms.

Vilification merely erects walls of animosity, alienates society from guidance and ultimately tarnishes the reputation of Islam itself. Indeed, Allah SWT explicitly prohibits Muslims from mocking, belittling and insulting others in Surah Al-Hujurat, verse 11, categorising such actions as reprehensible.
This mandate serves as evidence that Islam rigorously safeguards the harmony of speech in propagation for the broader public interest (maslahah).
This principle is further reinforced by the hadith of the Prophet Muhammad, narrated by Al-Tirmidzi: "A believer is not one who slanders, curses, speaks obscenely or engages in foul speech."
If insulting an ordinary individual is prohibited, how can the same tongue used for religious propagation justify vilification in the name of partisan differences?
Death transcends ideological boundaries
Despite the political tensions that frequently fracture societal structures, death serves as an absolute reminder that transcends all worldly boundaries.

Visiting the deceased – whether they were staunch supporters or the most vocal adversaries – is the highest manifestation of human value and fraternity. For a deceased Muslim, the visit constitutes the fulfilment of an obligatory right owed to a fellow Muslim.

What then is the protocol if the deceased is a non-Muslim? Islam never restricts the scope of compassion. History records the sublime character of the Prophet Muhammad, who stood up in respect for a passing Jewish funeral procession. When questioned by his companions, the Prophet replied profoundly: "Was it not a human soul?"

The presence of a leader or a preacher at the condolence gathering of a political adversary signifies emotional maturity and reflects the attribute of mercy (rahmah) capable of softening hardened hearts. Where politics constructs walls, the visitation of the deceased builds bridges.
Realigning politics with ethics
In conclusion, a preacher must position himself as an agent of unity and a harbinger of mercy, rather than a disrupter of social bonds (silaturahim).
Partisan politics and ideological differences are normal in a democratic system, but they must never undermine the ethical pillars of Islamic morality.

It is high time for practitioners of dakwah to push back against the tide of adversarial politics. Insults must cease, and human connections must be preserved, particularly during times of calamity and death.
Ultimately, religious propagation is judged by the beauty of its ethical character, whereas partisan politics will inevitably fade with time.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

96b8733b678ca1a7: The Sedition Act 1948 ought to be struck out unless Parliament amends the Federal Constitution to expressly incorporate it as a permitted restriction on free speech.
A colonial relic, the Sedition Act was enacted when the country was under imperial control.

It has survived almost 70 years since Merdeka not because of constitutional legitimacy but due to judicial pronouncements rooted in the outdated notion that Malaysia practised parliamentary supremacy.

That principle, prevailing in the UK, holds that Parliament has the ultimate legal authority to enact, amend or repeal any law, and that no other institution, not even the courts, has the power to override or invalidate its legislation.

On that basis, the Sedition Act had for decades lingered as a convenient instrument of state authority, defended on the premise that Parliament may restrict speech absolutely in the name of national security.
Since 2017, however, the Federal Court has firmly embraced constitutional supremacy, and under this doctrine, the Sedition Act can no longer stand.
Constitutional supremacy dictates that the Federal Constitution is the supreme law of the land. Any legislation, whether pre- or post-Merdeka, that conflicts with its spirit must be voided.
Article 10(2)(a) of the constitution permits restrictions on free speech, but only if they are reasonable and proportionate.
The Sedition Act fails this test.
Predating the constitution itself, it criminalises speech based on vague notions of “seditious tendency”, without requiring proof of intent to incite violence or disorder.
Such a law bypasses constitutional safeguards and undermines the very liberties the constitution guarantees.
The judiciary’s oath of office, prescribed by the constitution itself, provides further clarity. Judges do not swear allegiance to Parliament or the government of the day.
Their solemn oath is to preserve, protect and defend the constitution.

Judicial power, vested in the superior courts by the constitution, is not a passive instrument to rubber-stamp legislative excess. It is an active and inherent power that allows the courts to act as the ultimate check and balance.

When a law infringes upon fundamental liberties, the judiciary has a constitutional duty to intervene. To leave the Sedition Act intact merely because it has been historically preserved is to betray that oath.
The jurisprudential shift taken by the apex court leaves no room for ambiguity. The courts must now exercise their full constitutional judicial power to strike down the Sedition Act.
Doing so will dismantle a vestige of colonial control and affirm Malaysia’s commitment to governance under its own constitution.
The judiciary will also be viewed not merely as honouring its oath but as fulfilling the nation’s promise to uphold the true supremacy of its constitution.

7c50dabbb1470c30: The return of Bintulu Port to Sarawak after years of negotiations is more than a change in ownership. It raises a much bigger question about how Malaysia plans, funds and develops its strategic ports—and whether the same principles are being applied fairly across the country.
From Sept 1, Bintulu Port is officially under the ownership and management of the Sarawak government, following a negotiated agreement with Putrajaya.

The question that naturally follows is this: if Sarawak can take greater control of Bintulu Port, should other states also be given greater control over strategically important ports located within their territories?
The issue is not simply about who owns a port.
It is about who makes the decisions, who provides the money and, ultimately, who benefits from the economic development that the port generates.
The comparison between Bintulu Port in Sarawak and Kemaman Port in Terengganu is particularly revealing.
Bintulu not any port
Bintulu's development shows what can happen when port development is closely integrated with a state's natural resources and industrial ambitions.

Built in 1978, with the Bintulu Port Authority established in 1981 and operations commencing two years later, its development has been closely tied to the discovery and exploitation of offshore oil and gas resources in the Luconia Basin, off the coast of Sarawak.

The development of the liquefied natural gas (LNG) industry within the port transformed Bintulu. Gas was brought ashore to feed the LNG facilities, and the LNG export terminal became the foundation for a much larger industrial economy.
The port did not remain a simple facility for loading and unloading cargo. It expanded to handle liquid bulk, dry bulk and containerised cargo.
Industries developed around it. Infrastructure followed. The hinterland expanded. The township grew.
Today, Bintulu Port is one of Sarawak's most important economic assets, handling around 52 million tonnes of cargo in 2025. This serves as an important lesson.
A port is not merely a maritime facility. It can be the economic foundation upon which an entire industrial region is built, giving employment to practically everyone in the district.
Kemaman, another sleepy hollow
Kemaman, too, has a remarkable story.
The port was originally developed by the Terengganu state government in 1978, about the same time that the federal government planned Bintulu Port.
As a supply base (another name for an oil and gas port) serving Terengganu offshore, it took over the roles of the Loyang supply base in Singapore.
The state's intention was to support the emerging oil and gas industry, with the objective of turning it into a one-stop centre for the oil and gas development in the South China Sea.
It didn't go down that route as the federal government had other ideas and different ambitions for the area. Perwaja, the national iron and steel project, was located there instead.

A large tract of land that would have been more suitable for an oil and gas terminal (Penggerang, Johor eventually took over that role) was allocated to the steel mill, together with a dedicated iron ore import handling facility called the East Wharf.

With the harbour depth dredged to –18 metres, Kemaman Port became the deepest port in Malaysia at the time. Super large bulk carriers brought in iron ores from as far as Brazil and Canada. The sleepy Chukai town transformed into a crew recreational centre.

By 1991, the federal government had sunk so much investment into Kemaman Port that it had no option but to take over the management via the Kemaman Port Authority. That's how the state port became a federal port.

But the iron ore hype didn't last very long. Somehow, the steel making industry failed to take off. Soon after, the grand steel mill and the large East Wharf became idle, not for a couple of years but a couple of decades, before China steel came into the picture.

The harbour basin, once boasting a water depth of 18 metres, was bereft of large ore carriers. What remained were only offshore supply vessels, anchor-handling tugs, and the occasional offshore survey vessel—each requiring no more than six metres of depth.
The Scale Gap: Kemaman vs. Bintulu
Terengganu’s 5% oil royalty

Putrajaya may have national responsibilities, but it should not assume that a centralised decision made in their glass houses is automatically the best decision for every region or state. The era of "the government knows best" should be over.
The government should listen more, devolve more, and allow states to take greater responsibility for their own economic future.
But devolution without money is meaningless. You cannot tell a state to develop its own economy while withholding the financial resources that would allow it to do so.

This is why the 5% oil royalty payment matters. Terengganu should receive what it is legitimately entitled to under the oil royalty agreement—like Sabah and Sarawak, Malaysia's other two oil and gas producing regions.
And rather than allowing the issue to remain a perpetual political dispute, the federal government should resolve it decisively. If the 5% is due, pay it.

Then let Terengganu decide how best to use part of that revenue to strengthen its productive economic base. Kemaman Port would be an obvious candidate. The state could invest in port facilities, industrial land, logistics infrastructure and supporting utilities, once the funds are available.

The federal government can continue doing what it does best: providing national infrastructure such as the East Coast Expressway (LPT1) and East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) and ensuring national connectivity.
As of now, the ECRL spur line to Kemaman Port still only exists on paper; construction has not even started while the main line for passengers services is starting in January 2027.
Malaysia cannot seriously talk about balanced regional development while economic decision-making and financial resources remain heavily concentrated in Putrajaya.
Bintulu shows how sustained investment in a strategic port can transform a region. Kemaman, by contrast, has languished—remaining dormant and wasteful for many years.
What it needs is the financial capacity and the freedom to develop them properly.
The federal government has already recognised Bintulu's strategic importance and devolved its ownership back to the state. It should now recognise Kemaman's and do the same.

The question of whether the current state government is capable or competent enough, is a story for another day. In fact, the mistakes and errors of the past came from the same Putrajaya; so the pot can't be calling a kettle black.

Denying Terengganu its rightful 5% oil royalty—resources that belong to its people—and preventing the state from deciding how best to harness them for future economic growth amounts to gross negligence on Putrajaya’s part.
If the federal government believes in fair federalism, it should honour that commitment.
Let Terengganu invest the funds. Let Kemaman Port grow rather than choke it. Let investors decide whether the port is commercially viable.
And let the state, rather than Putrajaya, take greater responsibility for making it happen.
Bintulu has been given that opportunity. Kemaman deserves no less.

aac38c9e929796b3: AI is advancing at a breathtaking pace, and so are fears about its impact on jobs, especially for young people entering the labour market.

The tasks generative AI can increasingly perform—writing computer code, summarising documents, analysing data, and handling customer inquiries—are precisely those that often provide young workers with their first foothold in the workforce.

But warnings by some AI-industry leaders that entry-level white-collar jobs will be largely wiped out within a few years run well ahead of the evidence. While AI is beginning to affect some entry-level jobs, its effects remain limited and uneven, and there are few signs of economy-wide displacement.
In the US, for example, a recent study found no broad employment decline associated with AI exposure. What fell was employment among 22–25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations.
It now stands 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with the rate among young workers in less-exposed sectors. Weaker hiring, rather than layoffs, drove this shift.

But even this evidence should be interpreted cautiously. While entry-level hiring in AI-exposed occupations began weakening around 2022, before ChatGPT was released to the public, this probably did not reflect the rise of AI—which, at that point, had limited capabilities—so much as rising interest rates, post-pandemic adjustments, and remote work.

Moreover, though the decline in entry-level hiring by tech firms since 2024 might be attributable to AI, demand for tech workers outside the industry remains strong. And where AI usage primarily complements workers, rather than substituting for human tasks, employment is flat or rising.

More broadly, recent US data does not point to a youth-employment crisis. The unemployment gap between 20–24-year-olds and the overall workforce is near a multi-decade low. In other words, not every job is exposed to AI, and even those that are do not automatically imply displacement.

This is even more true beyond the US. A recent World Bank study found that, in high-income countries, online job postings in occupations vulnerable to AI substitution declined by 5.8% relative to less-substitutable occupations since ChatGPT’s release.

In middle- and low-income countries, the decline was statistically insignificant. Lower AI adoption, weaker digital infrastructure, and the larger share of manual work limit AI’s immediate potential for displacement in developing economies.

In Asia, AI’s labour-market effects differ sharply across countries. In South Korea, youth employment fell disproportionately in industries with high AI exposure in 2022–25, while employment among workers in their 50s increased.
But much like in the US, it is impossible to determine the extent to which this can be attributed to AI rather than to other economic, demographic, and labour-market changes.

The Asean economies have some exposure to AI. The International Labour Organization estimates that occupations with more than minimal exposure to generative AI accounted for 22.9% of Asean employment in 2025, but only 3.3% of the workforce was in jobs with the highest exposure.
There are signs of weaker employment growth among young workers in some exposed occupations and entry-level jobs, but no broader deterioration in labour-market outcomes for this age cohort.
In China, rapid AI deployment appears to be creating displacement pressures for some workers, ranging from taxi drivers to white-collar professionals.

This may well compound the challenges faced by young people entering the labour force, but China’s high youth unemployment predates the AI boom, reflecting slowing growth, private-sector weakness, and skills mismatches.

In India, by contrast, the risks are concentrated in the large information-technology and business-services sectors. While industry leaders dispute that AI is causing mass layoffs, there have been workforce reductions at major IT firms, and cross-country evidence suggests that economies specialising in digitally deliverable services may face greater employment pressure.

Japan’s situation is very different. With rapid population ageing implying severe labour shortages, AI looks less like a threat than a solution. Generative AI use remains relatively limited, suggesting that expanding productive adoption and worker training may be more pressing than preventing displacement.
Across Asia, greater efforts must be made to ensure that young people have the tools they need to engage productively with AI. Updating education and training programmes is essential.

Schools and universities must teach AI skills and digital literacy, as well as complementary skills that are harder to automate, such as analytical reasoning, judgment, communication, creativity, and teamwork. AI use must enhance learning, not substitute for it.

For those already in the workforce, firms must offer periodic retraining opportunities. As one OECD study showed, retraining, worker consultations, and clear workplace guidelines can go a long way towards harnessing AI-driven productivity gains.
As entry-level tasks are automated, firms must also provide internships, apprenticeships, and other work-based learning opportunities for younger workers.

The challenge is to use AI to strengthen human capital, rather than short-circuit its accumulation. My recent research finds that greater AI exposure in South Korea is associated with improvements in adult numeracy, with some evidence of larger gains among younger workers.

But no amount of AI training can substitute for robust labour-market institutions and sound economic policies. The details will differ across countries, but in general, labour-market rules should make it easier for firms to hire and train young workers. And macroeconomic stability, investment, entrepreneurship, and competition remain essential to creating productive jobs.
AI will almost certainly transform Asia’s labour markets, and young workers may feel the effects first. But the shift might not be as dramatic as some industry leaders would have us believe.
In any case, the best defense against AI-induced disruption lies in acquiring the skills, experience, and opportunities to use the technology well.

Lee Jong-Wha, professor of economics at Korea University, is a former chief economist at the Asian Development Bank and a former senior adviser for international economic affairs to the president of South Korea.

968cce7960281a8b: From Malik Ismail

A student in a hostel is told to fetch water for a senior after lights out. Another is expected to wait until everyone else has taken their bath. A third is mocked in front of the dormitory. He laughs with the others, although he is embarrassed, because he fears that objecting will make him a target again.

To an adult passing by, these may seem like unrelated moments. To a younger student, they can form a pattern. Someone else decides what you must do, when you may say no and whether your discomfort matters.

Bullying does not always announce itself through a fight. It can develop through repeated demands, jokes and small acts of control that become familiar to everyone around them. This is why a school’s response cannot begin only when an incident becomes severe. It begins with noticing what students have learned to accept.
When seniority becomes authority

Older students can do much to make newcomers feel welcome. They can explain routines, offer friendship and help a child adjust to life away from home. These are valuable parts of hostel life. The boundary is crossed when a senior begins to act as though age or experience gives them authority over another student’s time, belongings or dignity.

But the word "tradition" should never settle the question of whether a practice is acceptable. An errand may appear harmless, but could the junior refuse it? A nickname may draw laughter, but does the child who hears it every day find it funny? When students begin to treat informal power as permission to control others, who notices and intervenes?

The answer cannot be left to a frightened junior. Schools should state the boundary before it is crossed – seniors may guide, but they may not command, punish, humiliate or hurt. When a credible concern is raised, adults must establish the facts fairly and act on what they find. Zero tolerance is credible only when the rule is taught, applied consistently, and followed through.
The courage to report should be met with action

The education ministry has issued guidelines for managing bullying and provided an official complaints portal. The responsibility now falls on principals and headmasters to make those measures work in the daily life of each school and hostel. A child deciding whether to speak up is unlikely to think first about a guideline. The question is more immediate: Will telling someone make things worse for me?

The first adult to hear a concern may be a teacher, counsellor, warden, religious educator or parent. That adult should listen without dismissing the account as teasing, check whether the child is safe and ensure the concern reaches someone who can act. The principal or headmaster must ensure that the concern is recorded, examined fairly and addressed with appropriate protection.

That protection matters during the inquiry and afterwards. A child may face pressure to withdraw a complaint or fear returning to the same dormitory. Someone should check back privately to find out whether the intimidation has stopped. Students also need more than one trusted route to report a concern; no child should have to approach the person they fear.
Trust is built when a child sees what happens after speaking up – an adult listens, the school acts and someone returns to ask whether the child is safe.
Every adult has a part

Clear boundaries should be explained to students, parents and staff before hostel life begins, then reinforced throughout the year. Helping a newcomer is welcome. Personal errands imposed by seniors, private punishments, humiliating rituals, taking belongings and unwanted physical contact are not.

Principals set the expectation, but they cannot carry it alone. Wardens see students outside the classroom and may notice changes in sleep, friendships or behaviour. Teachers may see a child withdraw or struggle to concentrate. Counsellors can offer a private place to talk and help plan support. Prefects can model responsible leadership rather than enforce unofficial rules. Religious teachers and other trusted adults can reinforce the same message in their daily conversations with students.
Each adult needs to know when and how to pass on a concern. No one should assume that someone else has already done so.

This requires preparation, not simply a written policy. Training for educators, counsellors, wardens and school leaders should cover bullying, child development, trauma and the realities of residential life. Professional programmes can help them practise difficult conversations and coordinated responses. Knowing that a child should be heard is one thing; knowing how to listen when that child is frightened is another.
What we have learned to overlook

Children arrive at school with different experiences of respect and authority. Some are used to polite disagreement and clear personal boundaries. Others may have encountered harsh language or behaviour so often that it feels familiar. These differences are not grounds for judging children or their families. They are reasons to teach, demonstrate and uphold respectful conduct for everyone.

Adults, too, may remember rough experiences from their school days and believe those experiences made them stronger. A former student may look back fondly on a hostel ritual that a newcomer finds distressing. We can value the friendships that grow in schools without requiring today’s children to endure whatever previous generations endured. Traditions should be judged by whether they welcome and support students.

Parents can help by listening and not rushing to minimise or dramatise a child’s account. Ask what happened, whether it has happened before, and whether the child feels safe returning. Students who witness bullying should know they can alert an adult without having to confront a group alone.

A fair response also has room for the student who caused harm. The behaviour must stop, the affected child must be protected, and consequences must be appropriate. The student responsible may need guidance to understand the harm and change their conduct. Supporting that change does not lessen the school’s duty to protect the child who was hurt.

The strength of a school or hostel is often revealed before a crisis – a junior can decline an unreasonable request; a warden notices that a student has grown quiet; a teacher takes a troubling account seriously; a principal asks whether the child is still safe a week later.

These are ordinary acts of attention, carried through with responsibility. They are how adults make a rule against bullying meaningful, especially when small acts of intimidation happen again and again. A child should never have to wait for harm to become unmistakable before someone notices and acts.
Malik Ismail is a senior honorary lecturer in education and senior research fellow in the community engagement division at Universiti Sains Malaysia.

One more thing
A plan to make drugs in orbit is going commercial

A startup called Varda Space Industries is betting that the future of pharmaceuticals lies in orbit. The company has signed a deal with United Therapeutics to test whether drugs crystallize differently in microgravity, potentially creating improved versions with new properties.

The idea sounds futuristic, but falling launch costs and reusable rockets are making space-based manufacturing seem increasingly plausible. Varda says the partnership could mark an important step toward building products in orbit for use back on Earth.
Discover how space could become the next frontier for drug development.
—Antonio Regalado
